Agent Substrate

Sandboxing, Scheduling, and Multiplexing AI Agents on Kubernetes

Source-grounded manuscript · Refreshed for v1.0.0 · November 9, 2026

Implementation baseline: v1.0.0, commit b34fbee742906494b5eb4f1f36987176bf8770a4. The first edition was written against 0ddbf78d54bb6da2ccb01125b7e085aa14d555a6; this edition revises it against the release tag.

Preface

Substrate puts a second scheduling and lifecycle system above Kubernetes. Kubernetes provisions worker Pods and supplies the surrounding infrastructure. Substrate assigns actors to those workers, restores their execution state, mediates their network traffic, and moves their snapshots between local storage and an object store. Understanding that division requires following several kinds of state at once: PostgreSQL records, Kubernetes objects, node-local bookkeeping, sandbox processes, filesystem objects, and authenticated network sessions.

This book follows those state transitions through a specific checkout. Its central questions are concrete. Which write establishes an actor assignment? Which process may still use a snapshot file after a restore returns? What prevents a worker restart from accepting instructions for an earlier incarnation? Which memory charge can kill a neighboring actor? Where is an outbound request authenticated, and where is its credential added? What survives losing a node, and what survives losing an object-storage deployment?

The answers cross component boundaries. A scheduler policy cannot establish exclusive assignment without a store transaction. A fast restore does not establish readiness until the guest can service the wakeup probe. An object-store acknowledgment establishes only the durability offered by that configured backend. A private network namespace does not decide whether an actor may contact a particular hostname. The book therefore treats the system as cooperating protocols rather than a list of binaries.

The intended reader already understands Kubernetes control-plane internals, reconciliation, container construction, namespaces, cgroups, and virtualization. Basic explanations appear only where a distinction changes Substrate behavior. The emphasis is on actual structs, interfaces, algorithms, failure sequences, resource accounting, and the cost of maintaining consistency while many actors share a smaller worker fleet.

The source contract

Every implementation claim refers to the local repository baseline named above. Code links in the chapters point to the upstream repository at the v1.0.0 tag, so every reference resolves on GitHub without a local clone. Generated public and internal protocols, deployment manifests, dependency pins, benchmark harnesses, tests, and relevant vendored wrappers are part of the evidence. A comment or documentation page is not treated as proof when executable code contradicts it.

The v1.0.0 tree has 14,019 tracked files, including 11,645 under vendor/. Deep inspection concentrated on first-party behavior and the dependency boundaries it exercises. That does not mean every line of every vendored library was manually reviewed. The complete syscall behavior of Go, Envoy, runsc, Cloud Hypervisor, virtiofsd, and a selected CSI driver cannot be established by searching Substrate's Go files. Appendix A identifies direct calls, library-mediated calls, and external-runtime mechanisms separately.

The v1.0.0 revision is the first release covered by the README's compatibility commitment and by the version-skew policy, which applies from 1.0.0 and covers compatible releases only. Its architecture document no longer carries a planned status, but its targets remain targets. There is no docs/roadmap.md in this revision. Roadmap discussions therefore cite explicit targets, preview gates, limitations, or source TODOs, and identify additional proposals as proposals.

The book contains no new performance measurements. Numbers from flags, manifests, algorithms, and configuration are implementation facts at the baseline. North-star latency and scale numbers are targets. Historical benchmark observations are identified as such when discussed. Capacity examples are worked models with stated assumptions, not claims about a measured cluster.

What the book covers

Chapter 1 introduces Substrate's resource model and execution topology. Chapters 2 to 4 lay the foundation the rest of the book builds on: how containerd, runc and gVisor differ, how a Pod travels from kubectl apply through the API server, etcd, the scheduler and the kubelet, and how the node builds it on Linux with cgroups, namespaces, CNI, image unpacking and runc's system calls. Chapters 5 to 7 cover Substrate's control plane: its two API planes, placement and consistency in ateapi, and Kubernetes reconciliation. Chapters 8 to 11 descend to the node: node supervision, a complete trace of an actor's first start (the actor counterpart of Chapters 3 and 4), then the gVisor and microVM backends. Chapters 12 and 13 cover persistence: snapshot storage, then suspend and restore at the system-call level. Chapters 14 to 17 separate transport from authorization and credential handling, then cover measurement, operations, extension boundaries and upgrades.

Each chapter has six numbered sections. Section N.6 considers the subsystem's roadmap and engineering improvements. This keeps unfinished work adjacent to the mechanism it would change. The appendices collect the kernel audit, source inventory, implementation-status matrix, vocabulary, and a reference explaining every Linux command and system call used in Chapters 2 to 4, 9 and 13, with who calls it.

RustFS receives explicit treatment as an alternate object-store deployment through the S3 backend. The repository already includes a RustFS deployment, bucket-initialization Job, NetworkPolicy, and matching node/control plugin configuration for kind. Those files establish an integration path. Their single-replica deployment, small PVC, HTTP endpoint, and static development credentials do not establish a production availability or security design. The storage and operations chapters explain what changes when the object store shares infrastructure and failure domains with the compute fleet.

Reading the diagrams and examples

Mermaid diagrams express ordering, ownership, and boundaries. An arrow labeled with an RPC means a protocol invocation, not a claim that the associated state transition is atomic with every adjacent arrow. Database transaction boundaries and persistence points are identified explicitly when they matter. State diagrams abbreviate error handling only when the accompanying text explains the omitted branches.

Code excerpts illustrate actual implementation decisions. Pseudocode is labeled and should not be compiled as an API example. Operational commands are tied to the repository's current tooling; environment-specific values remain placeholders. Commands shown for a runbook are instructions for a prepared environment, not a record of commands executed while writing the manuscript.

The source links are pinned to the v1.0.0 tag, so they keep pointing at the same files. The companion and the reconnaissance notes are pinned to the first edition's commit, 0ddbf78d, because their evidence was captured there. The manuscript is intended to make such comparison easier: changes to schema ownership, worker admission, snapshot fidelity, runtime compatibility, or identity scope should be visible as changes to a specific contract, rather than as vague changes to an architectural description.

Publication and verification notes

This is a complete first manuscript, not a declaration that the software or prose has received an independent production certification. The publication checks verify chapter structure, source-link resolution, diagram rendering, cross-references, and actual word/page counts. They do not execute Kubernetes, KVM, CSI, cloud storage, or multi-node failure tests.

The project source retains its existing license and attribution. Short excerpts identify their source. No upstream source files were altered to make the narrative fit. The companion audit records important mismatches between older documentation and current behavior, including the conditional microVM demand-paging path and the absence of a wired automatic idle-suspension trigger.

1. Multiplexing Actors: Architecture and Execution Boundaries

1.1 The unit of persistence is not the unit of execution

Substrate separates an application's durable identity from the Kubernetes Pod that supplies its current execution capacity. The durable object is an Actor. The capacity object is a Worker, represented in Kubernetes by a worker Pod. An Actor can remain registered while it has no running processes, no active worker assignment, and no resident guest memory. When execution is required, Substrate assigns capacity in an existing worker and starts or restores the actor inside a sandbox. The Kubernetes Pod does not need to be created for that activation.

This separation is the architectural reason to build another control plane. It is also more precise than saying that Pods fail to scale. Kubernetes manages an infrastructure lifecycle with established admission, scheduling, node ownership, and reconciliation semantics. Substrate retains that machinery for worker capacity. It introduces a different lifecycle for applications whose useful execution is intermittent and whose state can survive as a checkpoint. The engineering question is whether moving that lifecycle above a warm worker fleet saves enough resources and latency to justify the additional consistency and storage systems.

The implementation makes a second distinction that is easy to miss: a worker can host multiple actors concurrently. Multiplexing is both temporal, as suspended actors reuse execution capacity later, and spatial, as several active sandboxes share one worker Pod. The scheduler tracks actor slots, CPU, and memory capacity. A worker is not simply marked occupied by one actor and returned to an empty pool at suspension. Each assignment books a share of its capacity, and releasing that assignment returns that share. The authoritative accounting resides in the worker and assignment records implemented by worker_assignment.go.

Consider a deliberately simplified capacity calculation. Let there be A registered actors, an active fraction f, a mean active application memory requirement m, and an additional sandbox overhead h. The memory associated with active execution is approximately A × f × (m + h), before adding workers, node supervisors, gateways, page cache, and storage buffers. A Pod-per-actor arrangement that keeps every application's memory resident pays a different cost even when CPU usage is near zero. This equation is a planning device, not a Substrate benchmark: independence between actors, average resource sizes, and stable demand are assumptions that a production workload may violate.

Suspension also has a cost. Every transition can consume CPU to serialize state, storage bandwidth to persist it, and time during which the application cannot serve requests. If an actor wakes repeatedly at short intervals, repeatedly checkpointing it can cost more than retaining its execution state. If a burst wakes most actors simultaneously, f approaches one and the density advantage shrinks. A fleet sized from the mean active fraction can therefore be incapable of serving its correlated peak. Request parking limits the immediate damage of a capacity shortage; it does not manufacture CPU, memory, or worker slots.

Resource accounting must include the runtime. scheduling.go adds a runtime-specific fixed memory overhead and a term proportional to actor memory to the requested limit. The runtime selected for a restored snapshot influences this booking. It would be incorrect to compare only application RSS across gVisor and microVM workers and then infer cluster capacity. Runtime processes, guest kernel memory, page tables, page cache, and transient checkpoint allocations can all affect the host while appearing in different accounting domains.

An Actor's logical continuity is consequently broader than process continuity. A MEMORY snapshot may restore an execution image. A ROOTFS restore preserves filesystem writes while cold-starting processes. A VOLUMES restore preserves selected durable directories while permitting a different application template to boot. The public API records the fidelity and runtime identity needed to interpret those outcomes. An application that requires instruction-level continuation must distinguish a memory restore from a restart that retains files; both can be legitimate Substrate lifecycle operations.

The actor abstraction is not an actor-language runtime. The repository does not require a mailbox, a single-threaded event loop, or application-level message passing. An actor is a sandboxed workload described by an ActorTemplate. Containers inside that workload can run ordinary applications, subject to the runtime and network contracts. A Jupyter server, a counter service, and an agent execution environment exercise different application behavior while using the same placement and suspend/resume APIs. The name identifies the lifecycle unit, not a concurrency model imposed on application code.

A useful planning model separates three populations: registered actors, active assignments, and ready worker capacity. Registered actors drive database and snapshot-retention costs. Active assignments drive sandbox execution and network costs. Ready capacity drives the ability to absorb activations without a Kubernetes provisioning delay. Those populations can differ by orders of magnitude, but their ratios are workload-dependent. A capacity dashboard that reports only worker Pod count cannot show whether a large registered population is cheap, whether active execution is near saturation, or whether snapshots are consuming the node's local storage budget.

The diagram shows a relationship, not a fixed density. Worker one has two independent active assignments. Actor delta consumes storage and metadata without an execution assignment. If delta resumes, its placement is selected from workers that satisfy selectors, runtime compatibility, locality, and remaining capacity. Its previous worker is neither its identity nor an unconditional destination.

1.2 Component topology and the two control loops

The local module is go.ate.dev/substrate. Its layout separates public APIs in api, command-specific code in cmd, shared implementation in internal, externally importable packages in pkg, and Kubernetes manifests in manifests. There is no ateom daemon in this revision. Runtime work is implemented by cmd/ateworker-gvisor and cmd/ateworker-microvm, with shared machinery under internal/ateworker. This naming matters because following an obsolete component diagram leads to the wrong ownership assumptions when investigating failures.

The Kubernetes-facing control loop starts with WorkerPool, SandboxConfig, and CSIDriverConfig resources in ate.dev/v1. WorkerPool specifies worker replicas and their configuration. atecontroller reconciles Deployments and supporting infrastructure, resolves SandboxConfig references, and synchronizes worker Pods with the Substrate worker registry. Kubernetes schedules those Pods and maintains their node-level container lifecycle. None of this removes kube-scheduler, kubelet, or the container runtime from the system. It moves their work to the capacity-provisioning timescale.

The actor-facing control loop runs in ateapi, deployed as ate-api-server. It exposes the public Control gRPC service and the component-facing WorkerService. Its PostgreSQL store holds actor records, worker records, assignments, tags, policies, and leases. Actor workflows select workers, change actor state, and call the node supervisor. The critical path for an actor activation therefore includes Substrate's own database and RPCs even when it avoids a Kubernetes write. Describing activation as control-plane-free would be misleading; it bypasses a particular control plane's provisioning path.

atelet runs as a DaemonSet. It connects the cluster-level actor workflows to workers on one node. It prepares images and runtime assets, coordinates snapshots and volumes, manages worker-facing support services, and advertises hardware devices through a kubelet device plugin. The worker processes implement the actual sandbox lifecycle. A worker exports internal gRPC operations including RunWorkload, CheckpointWorkload, RestoreWorkload, and TerminateWorkload. The intended separation is that atelet and the workers share protocol and path contracts without depending on each other's internal implementation.

Networking has its own topology. The atenet-router and atenet-egress deployment roles run shared atenet and Envoy machinery. Ingress external processing asks the control plane to resume or locate an actor, then forwards traffic to the appropriate worker tunnel. Egress enforcement evaluates actor-specific policy and can inject credentials outside the sandbox. atunnel is an embedded worker library, not a separately scheduled Kubernetes DaemonSet. Its position inside the worker is important: it connects a stable worker-facing transport to per-actor network namespaces whose contents change as actors start and stop.

The identity infrastructure is also explicit. podcertcontroller issues the certificates used by Substrate components through its configured signers. ate-idp-server exposes actor identity discovery material. Credential-provider implementations serve secrets to the egress path. These processes support execution but do not schedule actors. Treating them as incidental utilities hides availability dependencies: certificate issuance or rotation failures can prevent new authenticated connections even when workers and database capacity are healthy.

Snapshots cross an object-store plugin boundary. The control-plane sidecar implements whole-snapshot copy and cleanup operations; the node-side sidecar uploads and fetches snapshot files and fetches sandbox assets. The main ateapi process does not directly link the GCS or S3 storage SDKs, a rule enforced by package-deps.sh. This is more than packaging tidiness. It places provider credentials and provider-specific I/O in a process boundary, allowing the control plane to express storage operations through the public plugin protocol.

RustFS is an existing alternative backend in the kind deployment. Both node and control-plane object-store sidecars set ATE_STORAGE_BACKEND=s3, point AWS_ENDPOINT_URL at http://rustfs.ate-system.svc:9000, and enable AWS_S3_USE_PATH_STYLE. The RustFS manifest provisions the service, a one-replica deployment, a 1 GiB PVC, and bucket initialization. This is a concrete S3-compatible development and CI path. Its static development credentials and single storage replica do not establish production high availability or tenant isolation. Chapter 12 follows the actual data path and failure implications.

There are several loops behind this topology rather than one universal reconciler. The infrastructure controllers use controller-runtime. Worker Pod synchronization uses its own client-go informers and workqueue. Golden snapshot creation and worker-assignment recovery run inside ateapi using their own queues and persisted state. A failure analysis must first identify which loop owns progress. Restarting atecontroller cannot directly repair every stalled actor workflow, and watching a Kubernetes Deployment will not reveal every change to an actor assignment.

The distinction between command name and deployed service name is similarly practical. Source investigation starts in cmd/ateapi; cluster inspection usually finds ate-api-server. Runtime configuration can be supplied through flags, configuration protos, Kubernetes objects, and mounted identity files. The architecture should be understood through the concrete ownership of each value rather than inferred from binary naming alone. Later chapters trace those contracts at their validation and authentication boundaries.

1.3 Host, Pod, sandbox, and guest boundaries

A worker Pod is an infrastructure isolation and allocation unit. An actor sandbox is the execution isolation unit inside it. For gVisor, the application interacts with a userspace kernel, the Sentry, and associated filesystem machinery. For microVMs, the application interacts with a guest kernel, while Cloud Hypervisor and virtiofsd mediate host resources. The host Linux kernel still schedules the runtime processes, enforces their cgroups and capabilities, and supplies device and networking interfaces. The word kernel must identify which boundary is under discussion.

In the gVisor backend, runsc executes inside the worker and manages the actor sandbox. The worker invokes runsc lifecycle and checkpoint operations; it is not itself a replacement Sentry. Application syscalls handled inside gVisor do not all become identical host syscalls. Conversely, operations that the worker performs directly, such as creating network devices or preparing files, are host-kernel operations even though the eventual application is sandboxed. A syscall inventory that mixes those two layers cannot explain either isolation or latency.

The microVM backend drives a Kata guest model with Cloud Hypervisor. The worker arranges the VM, the guest agent connection, and the filesystems supplied to it. /dev/kvm is a host device boundary used by the VMM. TAP devices connect virtual networking to the actor's host-side network arrangement. Virtio-fs exposes host-backed filesystem state to the guest. The actor's process tree lives under a guest kernel whose memory and device state are part of the VM lifecycle, while the VMM remains a host process with its own resource consumption and failure modes.

The worker Pod security context is deliberately more capable than an ordinary application Pod. workerpool_apply.go sets both worker classes to nonprivileged, drops the default capability set, and adds explicit capabilities needed for runtime and network operations. It also sets AppArmor and seccomp profiles to Unconfined at the Pod container boundary. Runtime processes can apply their own confinement, but that is a separate claim from the Pod's outer profile. A nearby stale comment about runtime-default seccomp must not override the builder's actual output.

The difference matters during incident investigation. A capability such as CAP_NET_ADMIN enables the trusted worker to construct the actor's network environment. It should not be interpreted as an ambient capability granted to every actor process. A host /dev/kvm permission allows the VMM to establish virtualization; it is not evidence that an application inside the guest can open that host device. The security argument depends on which process receives which handle and on the runtime's subsequent confinement, not merely on a list of capabilities in a YAML document.

MicroVM workers request KVM as an extended resource served by atelet's device plugin. A hostPath mount alone would make a device inode visible without necessarily granting access through the container's device controls. The kubelet device-manager interaction supplies that access grant and makes KVM availability a placement constraint. By contrast, the current worker template bind-mounts /dev/net/tun and relies on the runtime's default device allowance plus network-administration capability for TAP creation. Both are host interfaces, but they enter the Pod through different mechanisms.

Actors also need isolation from one another inside a worker. Shared Pod networking would be insufficient if each sandbox directly inherited a common address space for network configuration. The gVisor worker creates two private network namespaces for each actor: a runtime namespace and a gateway namespace joined by a veth pair. This separation lets runsc take ownership of the runtime-side interfaces while atunnel serves the gateway side. The microVM worker instead puts a TAP interface and atunnel sockets in one host network namespace; the guest owns the other end of that network boundary. The resulting routes direct each actor through atunnel and the controlled egress path. The application is addressed through its actor identity at ingress, not by treating a Pod IP as a durable application endpoint. A worker's address can remain constant while its set of hosted actors changes.

Filesystem isolation follows a similar separation between shared preparation and private mutable state. An image cache can share immutable image content. A runtime asset cache can share verified executable assets by content identity. Each actor still needs distinct writable state and lifecycle cleanup. In microVMs, the writable rootfs upper is host-backed and served through virtio-fs, so its storage and page-cache effects differ from allocating equivalent data inside guest RAM. gVisor's filesystem checkpoint bundles have different mechanics. Architectural equivalence of the API does not mean identical memory accounting or snapshot layout.

The gVisor boundary places the application above the Sentry's syscall implementation. Runtime supervision and atunnel remain trusted host processes. A network namespace is a host-kernel object even when the actor's network stack is implemented by the Sentry.

The microVM boundary adds a guest kernel and virtual devices, with Cloud Hypervisor and virtiofsd mediating host resources. These diagrams describe alternative worker classes: a WorkerPool currently selects one sandbox class, and one worker image does not dynamically mix gVisor and microVM actors. Runtime-version compatibility remains a live concern within a class. A worker advertises which versions it can restore, and a snapshot records its capture runtime. That version boundary permits controlled upgrades without assuming every memory image is portable across executable revisions.

Trust also crosses process boundaries outside the worker. The node object-store plugin has storage credentials that atelet does not need to hold. The egress gateway can obtain a secret that the actor does not receive as an environment variable or mounted file. The control plane verifies component identities before accepting worker reports. These separations reduce particular exposures, but they create protocols that must authenticate the actor, worker, node, and resource incarnation correctly. Chapter 15 examines those checks rather than relying on a general zero-trust label.

1.4 Following one actor through the system

Start with an infrastructure operator who creates a WorkerPool and suitable SandboxConfig. The controller resolves the runtime configuration and creates worker capacity. Kubernetes schedules the Pods; atelet and the worker establish their internal relationship; the worker registers its current epoch, runtime information, and capacity. Only then is that capacity eligible for actor placement. A Pod's mere existence is insufficient. A ready infrastructure object and a registered runtime process are related observations, not interchangeable facts.

An application operator creates an ActorTemplate through the Substrate API. The template describes containers, resources, volumes, selectors, probes, and snapshot behavior. It is stored in PostgreSQL. Where golden snapshot generation is enabled, the ActorTemplateReconciler in ateapi drives a temporary golden actor through execution and snapshot creation. This is an asynchronous controller of its own. A client creating an actor must not assume that a golden image exists solely because the template record was accepted.

Creating an Actor establishes the logical identity and initial suspended state. Depending on its source and the template's state, it can refer to reusable snapshot content or have no snapshot to restore. The latter is supported explicitly: ensureAteletRestored chooses an atelet Run request when snapshotToResume is nil. Golden snapshots accelerate a path; they are not a prerequisite for the existence of every actor. The distinction is visible in lifecycle telemetry, which classifies a cold boot separately from local and external snapshot restores.

An ingress client supplies ate-target-actor as an atespace/name reference. The HTTP Host field retains its application-authority meaning. The router asks ateapi to resume the actor and obtain an assignment. For an already-running actor, the API can return its record without performing a new distributed-lease write. For a suspended actor, it acquires the actor lease, reads authoritative state, and selects a compatible worker with capacity. Candidate selection uses an in-memory worker view; admission is rechecked against the database row before the booking commits.

The selected worker identifies a node, and the API calls that node's atelet. Atelet prepares the workload and its state, then calls the worker's runtime interface. A restore can use node-local files or fetch external snapshot data through the object-store sidecar. The chosen runtime starts or restores the sandbox, and the worker activates the actor's network path. The API finalizes RUNNING with the returned worker epoch. Only after successful activation does the router forward the original request to the assignment it received.

An explicit suspend reverses the resource commitment without deleting the actor. The API serializes the operation with the actor lease, marks SUSPENDING, asks atelet to checkpoint, coordinates external volume detachment, records snapshot state, and releases the active worker assignment. Asynchronous durability allows the API to return once a local checkpoint exists while upload proceeds in the background. Synchronous durability waits for the external upload. Either mode must distinguish process cessation, local checkpoint completion, and durable publication; those are different events with different failure consequences.

The current runtime does not autonomously detect actor idleness and issue that suspend. The repository contains a reusable upward RequestActorSuspend path in internal/ateworker/suspend, atelet, and WorkerService, but no production worker constructs the requester. Demos sometimes describe idle suspension in broad terms while their runnable steps invoke kubectl ate suspend. A higher-level orchestrator can call the API according to its own application policy. Automatic idle detection remains unfinished; capacity reclamation currently follows an explicit lifecycle request.

A subsequent resume prefers the newest state that remains usable. Locality can pin the actor to a node, avoiding an external download. If that node has no capacity, the workflow can detach the local snapshot, ensure the necessary external state is available, and retry placement elsewhere. If a required runtime version has no room, the supported fallback can restore filesystem state and cold-boot instead of restoring memory. A changed template can require VOLUMES fidelity. These transitions explain why state location, runtime compatibility, and application continuity must be considered together.

Deletion is another workflow rather than a single row removal. A running sandbox must be terminated, volumes must be detached, and capacity must be released before the logical object can safely disappear. Snapshot cleanup is part of resource reclamation, with explicit error handling and remaining garbage-collection TODOs. Revert is distinct from deletion: it abandons current execution or local progress in favor of a completed durable snapshot. These operations are introduced here to make failure semantics visible; Chapter 6 treats execution consistency, and Chapter 12 treats snapshot ownership and durability.

1.5 Reading performance and failure domains correctly

The shortest activation path and the most expensive activation path traverse the same named components but perform very different work. An already-running request needs identity checks, a control-plane lookup, and routing. A local memory restore may avoid object storage. An external restore downloads state. A runtime-incompatible snapshot may cold-boot from filesystem state. A brand-new actor without a golden snapshot may need image preparation and application startup. Reporting one resume number without describing these cases obscures the operating envelope.

The repository's architecture document sets north-star targets of 100 ms activation at the 95th percentile, one billion actors, and 1000 wakeups per second. At v1.0.0 the document no longer carries a planned status, but these values remain targets. They are not measurements produced by this manuscript. The source contains benchmarks and historical analysis, and no cluster was run for this book refresh. A production claim requires a workload definition, hardware and runtime versions, storage placement, cache state, concurrency, and an actual distribution of end-to-end observations.

A useful latency decomposition starts at request arrival and ends when the actor can receive traffic. It includes gateway parsing and authorization, API work, any waiting for capacity, lease and transaction latency, node RPCs, snapshot preparation, runtime restore, readiness or wakeup checks, and tunnel establishment. Some spans overlap; others serialize. Adding component averages does not reconstruct a percentile of the combined path. Likewise, a benchmark statistic expressed as mean plus two standard deviations is not a measured p95. Heavy tails and multimodal restore classes make that approximation especially unreliable.

Capacity and latency interact. The scheduler spreads work using a power-of-two-choices policy across eligible workers, but it cannot compensate for a pool whose constraints leave only one feasible destination. A snapshot's locality can concentrate demand on a node. Runtime compatibility can fragment otherwise available memory. Actor slot limits can reject an actor even when CPU is free. CPU and memory requests can leave unusable fragments after heterogeneous bookings. These are properties of the placement problem, not necessarily evidence that kube-scheduler has provisioned the wrong Pods.

Request parking makes the gateway's behavior under temporary exhaustion part of the resource model. Waiting requests consume gateway state and retain clients. Limits and deadlines determine whether a burst is absorbed, delayed, or rejected. A successful response after parking may have a very different latency from an immediate activation. Operational dashboards should separate time waiting for capacity from time restoring a sandbox; otherwise storage tuning can be attempted for a problem caused by insufficient worker supply. Chapter 14 follows the parking implementation and its bounded behavior.

PostgreSQL is a central failure domain for actor state. The implementation supports multiple API replicas, but replicas sharing one database do not eliminate the database dependency. The worker cache reduces repeated fleet reads during candidate selection; it does not allow authoritative admission to proceed safely without the store. Renewable leases, row locks, unique assignment records, and versions protect different invariants. They also consume queries and transactions. Database latency under contention can dominate a path whose runtime restore is fast.

The node is a different failure domain. A local checkpoint can be available before its upload finishes. Losing that node can therefore lose the newest local state even while an older durable snapshot remains. A background upload delay changes the exposure window as well as performance. Keeping state local improves reuse latency but ties availability to the node until durability and detachment conditions are met. A one-node RustFS development deployment can share the cluster's failure domain with its workers; moving snapshots through an object API alone does not prove physical independence.

A worker-process restart is narrower than a node failure but still destroys execution owned by the old process. Worker epochs let the control plane distinguish those incarnations. An actor record that says RUNNING under an earlier epoch must not be treated as proof that the replacement process still hosts it. Recovery reconciles those assignments and records crashes where necessary. Pod UID, worker epoch, actor UID, resource version, and snapshot generation each answer a different identity or ordering question. Collapsing them into a single generation concept loses the ability to explain several restart races.

The gateways add both policy and availability dependencies. Ingress authentication can reject a client before actor routing. Egress can deny a destination or fail credential acquisition even while the actor's processes are healthy. A timeout can occur in the HTTP transport rather than the sandbox. Because atunnel is embedded in the worker, worker restarts affect both execution and its tunnel endpoint. Because the external router is separate, it can remain healthy while every suitable worker is full. Diagnosis needs the complete request path and the relevant identity, not merely Pod phase.

There is also a software-supply boundary around runtime assets. SandboxConfig records verified content identities and supported versions. Atelet prepares those assets and workers report the runtimes they can use. An installation with healthy worker Pods but missing or invalid assets is not ready capacity. Conversely, changing a default runtime should not silently reinterpret an existing memory checkpoint. The runtime-version contract is therefore part of availability engineering as well as execution security. Chapter 8 covers asset caching, and Chapter 17 covers compatibility across upgrades.

A practical architectural review follows ownership rather than component count. For each action, identify the durable record, the process authorized to change it, the lock or precondition protecting concurrent changes, the external side effect, and the recovery path after a lost response. Apply that test to assignment, checkpoint upload, worker registration, credential minting, and runtime selection. Where the repository has only a TODO or an assumed reentrancy property, retain that limitation in the model. A diagram should make the uncertainty discoverable instead of smoothing it away.

A concrete capacity and failure exercise

Consider an example installation with two worker nodes and one WorkerPool. Each worker advertises several actor slots and a finite CPU and memory budget. Three actors are running, while a fourth is suspended with its newest checkpoint local to the first node. These numbers are illustrative. The example is intended to expose ownership boundaries, not to recommend a pool size or claim a measured concurrency limit.

A request for the suspended actor reaches the router while the first node's compatible workers have no room. The router cannot fix that condition by choosing a different Pod address: the control plane owns assignment and knows the snapshot's locality. The resume workflow first attempts placement under the local constraint. If it decides to detach from the full node, it checks for capacity elsewhere, asks atelet to release the local binding according to the snapshot state, and then retries assignment. The destination is not reserved before that detachment, so another activation can consume the available capacity in the meantime. The code records this race explicitly in detachFromFullNode (workflow_resume_detach.go); the actor can be left durable-only and need a later retry.

That outcome is acceptable only if the snapshot durability contract remains intact. It may increase latency, but it must not turn an unavailable local file into an assumed completed external checkpoint. The node supervisor's reported snapshot state and the object-store publication rules determine whether detachment is safe. A gateway that parks the request can wait for a subsequent placement opportunity, but parking must not conceal a permanently missing snapshot. Transient resource exhaustion and loss of the required state are different errors with different recovery actions.

Now suppose the selected worker process restarts after its node has accepted the restore request. The Pod may retain its UID and IP while the process obtains a new epoch. A response associated with the earlier epoch cannot be treated as proof of execution under the new one. Registration and assignment reconciliation provide a way to identify that discrepancy. An operator observing only the Pod's Running phase would miss the relevant transition. The actor's assignment and worker epoch are the records that connect the logical application to the process incarnation that actually executed it.

Alternatively, suppose the API replica loses its connection after the worker has successfully restored the actor but before the final RUNNING write reaches the caller. Retrying the request is not the same as starting a second actor. The workflow must recover persisted progress, honor an existing claim, and repeat only operations that are safe under their identity keys. The architecture therefore depends on contracts at both sides of the RPC, not just on the API's lease. A client deadline ending does not roll back a sandbox that another process has already created. Chapter 6 examines which state is persisted at each seam and where comments still call out reentrancy work.

Finally, suppose object storage becomes unavailable after several asynchronous suspends. The workers may already have released active execution capacity while atelet retains local checkpoints and retries uploads. The cluster can appear computationally healthy while its durability exposure grows. Additional activations on the same node may remain fast, making an average latency metric look reassuring. A node loss during that period has a different consequence from a node loss after completed uploads. Operations must therefore track checkpoint publication and local retention alongside request success.

The exercise illustrates why fault injection should be organized around transitions rather than only around process names. Killing an API replica before a lease is acquired, after a worker claim commits, after an RPC succeeds, and after final state persistence tests four different recovery obligations. The same applies to a worker restart before registration, during restore, and after an actor becomes RUNNING. A production test plan should choose those interruption points from the source-level sequence and inspect the resulting durable records. Generic restart tests are useful, but they cannot establish all of these invariants by themselves.

1.6 Roadmap and engineering improvements

The repository-backed roadmap begins with distinctions between goals and working code. The architecture document names activation latency, actor scale, and wakeup throughput targets. Its v1.0.0 text no longer lists autoscaling or peer state sharing as open problems, so the gaps below come from the source rather than from that document. Each target should be linked to the current implementation and to the measurements still needed to demonstrate it.

Automatic idle suspension is one such gap. The upward suspend request plumbing already exists, including retry policy and worker/node authorization. A future detector must decide what idleness means for an actor with concurrent requests, outbound connections, background computation, and several containers. It must avoid holding locks needed by the downward checkpoint operation. It must also account for stale idleness signals: work can arrive between detection and suspension. The current request helper deliberately limits retries because a past idleness observation loses meaning over time. Wiring a timer to it would not by itself establish a correct application policy.

Worker autoscaling is another architectural extension rather than a property implied by using Deployments. WorkerPool has a replica count and generated workloads can use familiar Kubernetes capacity mechanisms, but the audited source does not justify claiming a complete actor-demand-driven autoscaler. A useful future design would distinguish ready slots from raw Pod count, incorporate runtime compatibility and snapshot locality, and decide how much idle reserve to maintain. Scaling down would need to coordinate drain, active assignments, local snapshots, and external durability instead of simply deleting apparently quiet Pods.

Peer state sharing could reduce dependence on one node's local checkpoint, but it would introduce another publication and ownership protocol. A second copy is useful only if the system can identify which generation is complete, verify its contents, and retrieve it after the original owner disappears. Replication traffic competes with checkpoint and activation traffic. A production design would need explicit acknowledgment semantics, placement across failure domains, and rules for garbage collection. The existing object-store interface and snapshot metadata provide context, but they are not an implementation of peer replication.

The runtime roadmap also requires precision. Conditional userfaultfd-based microVM restore and sparse delta merging exist, but the default Cloud Hypervisor version currently selects eager Copy restore because of the observed prefault behavior recorded in the code. The architectural promise should therefore be bounded by runtime version and restore mode. A general claim that microVM resumes always demand-page would erase the actual compatibility decision. A future improvement can change that default after evidence supports it, while preserving a traceable relation between configuration, code, and benchmark results.

Several engineering improvements in this book are proposals rather than repository commitments. One is an activation classification carried consistently through logs and metrics: already-running, cold boot, local restore, remote restore, and fidelity fallback, with capacity waiting measured separately. Another is a fleet model that reports compatible available capacity for major runtime versions instead of only aggregate resources. A third is an operator-visible statement of local-only snapshot exposure, so delayed durability is treated as an explicit operational choice rather than discovered during a node loss.

A final proposal is to maintain an executable architecture inventory alongside release artifacts. That inventory would name the served RPCs, generated Kubernetes resources, runtime assets, identity authorities, and enabled preview features for a particular build. The repository already has code generation, dependency checks, pinned images, and metric registries that can supply much of the evidence. Connecting them would reduce drift between diagrams and deployment reality. It would also make the distinction between a public contract and an internal convention easier to review when new runtimes or storage providers are added.

The rest of the book proceeds from these boundaries. Its claims are anchored to the audited revision rather than to a hypothetical completed architecture. Where a mechanism is implemented, the following chapters trace the state and calls that make it work. Where behavior is conditional, the condition stays visible. Where the code identifies unfinished work, the analysis treats it as an engineering problem with specific invariants and failure cases, not as an existing guarantee.

Source map

  • Architecture document: workload model, component vocabulary, and north-star targets.
  • Resource model: separation of PostgreSQL API records and Kubernetes CRDs.
  • Scheduler: concurrent actor capacity, constraints, utilization, and runtime overhead.
  • Resume workflow: cold boot versus restore, assignment, fidelity fallback, and activation completion.
  • Resume detach: releasing a full node binding so placement can retry.
  • Worker Pod construction: security contexts, devices, mounts, and class-specific requirements.
  • Worker suspend requester: implemented upward request helper and limits of idleness-based proposals.
  • RustFS deployment and node sidecar overlay: the existing S3-compatible development topology.
  • Dependency boundary verification: enforced separation between ateapi and object-storage SDKs.

2. Container Runtimes: containerd, runc, gVisor and runsc

Chapter 1 described Substrate as a topology of components. Before following how those components place, start and suspend actors, this chapter and the next two establish what happens beneath an ordinary Kubernetes Pod. Every Substrate worker is such a Pod, and every actor mechanism is easiest to understand against that baseline. Chapter 3 follows one Pod from kubectl apply through the control plane to its node, and Chapter 4 builds it on Linux. Chapters 9 and 13 later follow an actor through first start, suspend and restore at the same level of detail, naming every component, protocol, command and Linux primitive on the way. This chapter supplies the vocabulary: the four programs that turn an OCI image and a specification into isolated execution, and how they differ.

Two kinds of statement appear in these foundation chapters. Behaviour of containerd, runc, gVisor, the kubelet and the Linux kernel is described from their upstream designs and documented interfaces; this repository does not implement it and its exact details move with their releases. Behaviour of Substrate is grounded in source at the v1.0.0 tag and linked. Where the two meet, the text says which side owns the step.

2.1 The layered runtime stack beneath a Pod

A Kubernetes node runs a stack of runtimes, each with a narrower job than the one above it.

Layer Example program Input it consumes What it produces
Node agent kubelet Pod objects from the API server CRI calls, volumes, cgroup parents, status
CRI runtime containerd with its CRI plugin CRI gRPC requests Images, snapshots, sandboxes, tasks
Runtime shim containerd-shim-runc-v2, containerd-shim-runsc-v1 Task API calls over ttrpc A long-lived parent for container processes
OCI runtime runc, runsc An OCI bundle: config.json plus a root filesystem A process (or sandbox) with namespaces, cgroups and security settings
Kernel Linux System calls The actual isolation and resource control

The Container Runtime Interface (CRI) is a gRPC protocol that the kubelet speaks over a Unix domain socket, conventionally /run/containerd/containerd.sock. Its RuntimeService contains sandbox and container operations such as RunPodSandbox, CreateContainer, StartContainer, StopPodSandbox and ContainerStatus; its ImageService contains PullImage, ImageStatus and RemoveImage. The kubelet does not know how to create a namespace, unpack a layer or call pivot_root. It asks the CRI runtime for sandboxes and containers and supervises the answers.

The Open Container Initiative (OCI) defines two contracts beneath that. The image specification describes manifests, configurations and content-addressed layers. The runtime specification describes a bundle: a directory holding config.json, which lists the process arguments, environment, user, mounts, namespaces, cgroup path, capabilities, seccomp filter, rlimits and annotations, plus a root filesystem. An OCI runtime is any program that implements create, start, state, kill and delete over such a bundle. runc and runsc both satisfy that contract. That is why one node can run ordinary and gVisor Pods side by side, selected through a RuntimeClass whose handler names a containerd runtime configuration.

The shim deserves attention because it explains process ownership. containerd does not parent container processes. For each sandbox it starts a shim binary, which daemonizes, listens on its own ttrpc socket and becomes the parent and child subreaper of the processes the OCI runtime creates. containerd can then restart without killing workloads. The shim holds the container's stdio pipes, collects exit statuses with wait4, and reports task events back to containerd. For runc, one containerd-shim-runc-v2 process typically serves every container in one Pod. For gVisor, containerd-shim-runsc-v1 plays the same role but drives runsc.

Substrate uses this stack exactly once per worker: the worker Pod itself is an ordinary Kubernetes Pod, created by the kubelet and containerd, and run by the node's default OCI runtime. Actors do not pass through the kubelet or containerd. The gVisor worker invokes runsc directly against bundles it prepares, as Chapter 9 shows. The book follows both paths so they can be compared step by step.

2.2 containerd: images, snapshots, sandboxes and tasks

containerd is a daemon with a plugin architecture. Its CRI plugin translates CRI requests into calls on internal services, and the services are useful to know by name because their state is visible on disk and through the ctr tool.

The content store holds immutable blobs addressed by digest, under /var/lib/containerd/io.containerd.content.v1.content/blobs/sha256/. A pull resolves an image reference to a manifest or an index, chooses the platform-specific manifest, then fetches the configuration and each layer blob. Every blob is verified against its digest before it is committed. Writes use ingest files and are renamed into place only after verification.

The metadata store is a bbolt database that records images, containers, snapshots, leases and namespaces (containerd namespaces, not Linux namespaces; the CRI plugin uses the k8s.io namespace). Garbage collection walks references from this database; a lease protects in-progress content from collection during a pull.

The snapshotter turns layers into filesystems. The default overlayfs snapshotter stores each layer as a directory under /var/lib/containerd/io.containerd.snapshotter.v1.overlayfs/snapshots/<id>/fs. Unpacking applies a layer's tar stream into a new active snapshot whose parent is the previous layer, then commits it. Committed snapshots are immutable and shared by every container that uses the layer. When a container is created, the snapshotter prepares one more active snapshot, the writable layer, and returns a mount list rather than mounting anything itself: typically a single overlay mount with lowerdir set to the colon-separated committed layers, upperdir to the new layer's fs directory and workdir to a scratch directory. Whiteout files in layers, character devices with device number 0/0, are how overlayfs represents deletions; opaque directories carry the trusted.overlay.opaque extended attribute.

The sandbox concept groups a Pod's containers. For a runc Pod, the CRI plugin's sandbox controller creates a network namespace, calls CNI, and runs the pause container that pins the Pod's shared namespaces. For a gVisor Pod, the same requests produce a gVisor sandbox: one Sentry kernel that will host every container in the Pod.

The task service is the live-process view. A container is metadata; a task is its running instance. CreateContainer in CRI becomes a container record plus a task create through the shim; StartContainer becomes a task start. The shim mounts the rootfs that the snapshotter described into the bundle's rootfs directory, writes config.json, and calls the OCI runtime.

Operators meet these concepts through three CLIs. crictl speaks CRI, so it sees what the kubelet sees: Pod sandboxes, containers, images and their status. ctr speaks containerd's native API and exposes content, snapshots, leases and tasks. nerdctl offers a Docker-like interface over the same daemon. The lifecycle companion's network collector uses crictl inspect to obtain the node-visible PID of the worker container, which is the bridge from Kubernetes identities to /proc and nsenter.

2.3 runc: the OCI runtime that uses the host kernel directly

runc is the reference OCI runtime, built on the libcontainer Go library with a small C component. It configures the host kernel to isolate a process and then gets out of the way: after execve, the container's process makes ordinary system calls that the host kernel services directly. Namespaces limit what it can see, cgroups limit what it can consume, and capabilities, seccomp, LSM profiles and no_new_privs limit what it can ask the kernel to do.

runc separates creation from start so that a supervisor can complete setup, such as network attachment, before user code runs.

  1. runc create <id> reads config.json, creates a state directory under its root (by default /run/runc/<id>), and opens a socket pair to communicate with the child it is about to make.
  2. It re-executes itself as runc init. Early in that process, a C constructor known as nsexec runs before the Go runtime starts threads. That timing matters: setns into a mount or user namespace and unshare of several namespace types require a single-threaded caller, which a running Go program never is.
  3. nsexec joins any namespaces given by path in the specification with setns. A Pod container joins the pause container's network, IPC and UTS namespaces this way. It then creates the remaining new namespaces with unshare or clone, using flags such as CLONE_NEWNS, CLONE_NEWPID, CLONE_NEWCGROUP, CLONE_NEWUTS, CLONE_NEWIPC and, when requested, CLONE_NEWUSER. A new PID namespace takes effect only for children, so nsexec forks again so that the eventual workload is PID 1 of its namespace.
  4. The parent runc places the child in its cgroup by writing its PID to cgroup.procs under the path from linux.cgroupsPath, through systemd when the systemd cgroup driver is used, and applies limits such as memory.max, cpu.max and pids.max.
  5. Inside the child, Go code prepares the root filesystem. It makes mount propagation private or slave so container mounts do not leak to the host, bind-mounts the rootfs onto itself, performs each mount from the specification (proc, sysfs, /dev as tmpfs, device nodes, /dev/pts, /dev/shm, mqueue, bind-mounted volumes), and then switches root with pivot_root(".", ".") followed by a lazy umount2(".", MNT_DETACH) of the old root. chroot is used only when pivot_root cannot be, for example on a ramfs root.
  6. It sets the hostname, applies rlimits, OOM score and sysctls, masks and makes read-only the sensitive /proc and /sys paths listed in the specification, then drops privileges: prctl(PR_SET_NO_NEW_PRIVS), capability bounding set reduction, capset, setgroups, setgid and setuid, LSM profile selection through /proc/self/attr/..., and finally installs the seccomp filter with seccomp(SECCOMP_SET_MODE_FILTER).
  7. runc init then blocks opening a FIFO named exec.fifo in the state directory. runc create exits, leaving a fully configured but not yet running process.
  8. runc start <id> opens the FIFO from the other end. The blocked init process proceeds to execve the user's command, replacing itself with the workload.

runc also protects itself. Because the container could otherwise overwrite the runc binary through /proc/self/exe during runc init, current releases execute from a protected copy or sealed descriptor rather than the on-disk binary. The details vary with the release, but the lesson is general: an OCI runtime executes inside a boundary it is still constructing.

2.4 gVisor and runsc: a user-space kernel behind the same interface

gVisor also implements the OCI runtime contract, as runsc, but places a different boundary between the workload and the host. The workload does not make system calls to the host kernel. It makes them to the Sentry, a Linux-compatible kernel written in Go that runs as an ordinary, heavily confined host process. The Sentry implements processes, threads, signals, virtual memory, filesystems, pipes, sockets and much of /proc itself, and calls the host kernel only through a small, filtered set of system calls.

A gVisor sandbox has several host processes.

Process Started by Role
runsc command The caller: a containerd shim, or Substrate's worker Executes one OCI command, such as create, start, checkpoint or restore, then exits
Sentry (runsc boot) runsc create The application kernel; services every application syscall
Gofer (runsc gofer) runsc create A file proxy that opens host files on the Sentry's behalf and serves mount points
Application stubs The Sentry, under the systrap platform Host processes that provide address spaces in which application code runs

The platform determines how application code is executed and how its system calls reach the Sentry. Under systrap, the default in current releases and the platform observed in this book's live experiment, application threads run in stub processes whose seccomp filter returns SECCOMP_RET_TRAP for application system calls. The resulting SIGSYS is handled by code that hands the call to the Sentry through shared memory, and the Sentry switches contexts without ptrace stops on the fast path. The older ptrace platform used PTRACE_SYSEMU and is slower. The KVM platform runs the Sentry as a guest-mode kernel and uses hardware virtualization for address spaces. It needs /dev/kvm, but is not a virtual machine monitor with a guest Linux.

Memory belongs to the Sentry. Application memory is backed by a single memory file, a host file created with memfd_create, from which the Sentry allocates pages and maps them into the stub address spaces with mmap. From the host's point of view, an application page is a page of that file. This is why gVisor can checkpoint an application's memory by writing out the populated regions of one file, without inspecting foreign host processes.

Filesystems are mediated. With directfs, the default in current releases, the gofer opens files and donates host file descriptors to the Sentry over a Unix socket, after which the Sentry performs I/O directly with calls such as pread and openat relative to those descriptors. The Sentry itself runs chrooted into an empty directory, so it cannot name host paths. Writable overlays for a container's root filesystem can be backed by memory or by a host file. Durable filesystem state can be checkpointed with the rest of the sandbox.

Networking can be sandbox-mode, where the Sentry runs its own TCP/IP stack (netstack) and exchanges raw frames with the network namespace's interface, or host-mode, where it forwards socket calls to the host. In sandbox mode, the host namespace keeps the interface but the Sentry owns the addresses and routes. That is exactly why the lifecycle experiment found only loopback routes in an actor's runtime namespace after runsc took it over.

runsc supports Kubernetes Pods by grouping containers into one sandbox. When containerd's CRI plugin creates the Pod's first container, it annotates the OCI specification with io.kubernetes.cri.container-type: sandbox. Subsequent containers carry container-type: container and an io.kubernetes.cri.sandbox-id naming the sandbox. runsc reads these annotations: the sandbox container boots a Sentry, and later containers are created inside that same Sentry rather than as new sandboxes. Substrate uses the same mechanism without containerd. ShapeGVisor sets io.kubernetes.cri.container-type to sandbox for the reserved _sandbox container and to container for each application, with io.kubernetes.cri.sandbox-id pointing at _sandbox. It also emits dev.gvisor.spec.mount.<name>.* annotations so a durable directory mounted by several containers is presented as one shared filesystem.

runsc commands also go beyond the OCI minimum, and those additions are the reason Substrate uses gVisor. runsc checkpoint serializes a running sandbox's kernel state and memory into image files. runsc restore builds a new sandbox from them. runsc fscheckpoint saves filesystem state without memory, and runsc wait -restore reports when background page loading completes. Chapters 10 and 13 cover how Substrate drives them.

2.5 Comparing runc and runsc where it matters

The following comparison is about isolation and lifecycle mechanics, not marketing performance numbers.

Property runc runsc (gVisor)
Who services application syscalls The host Linux kernel The Sentry, a user-space kernel
Host kernel attack surface exposed to the workload All syscalls not blocked by the seccomp profile The Sentry's own filtered syscall set; application syscalls never reach the host directly
Process view from the host Workload processes are host processes in new namespaces Workload processes exist only inside the Sentry; the host sees Sentry, gofer and stub processes
Root filesystem overlayfs mount prepared by the shim, entered by pivot_root Served by the gofer or directfs; the Sentry presents its own VFS
Networking Host kernel stack inside the Pod's network namespace netstack inside the Sentry, attached to the namespace's interface, or host passthrough
/proc and /sys Host kernel views, masked and read-only where configured Sentry-synthesized views
Memory accounting Workload pages charged to the container cgroup Sentry memory file and Sentry overhead charged to the sandbox cgroup
Checkpoint/restore Optional, through CRIU, which uses ptrace and /proc to capture host processes Native: the Sentry serializes its own state and memory file
Compatibility Native Linux behaviour Very broad but not complete Linux ABI; some syscalls, ioctls and /proc files differ
Typical overhead Syscall cost close to native Additional cost per syscall and for I/O-heavy workloads; memory overhead for the Sentry
Kubernetes integration Default runtime handler RuntimeClass handler runsc, containerd-shim-runsc-v1

Three differences shape the rest of the book.

First, what a namespace means differs. Under runc, the network namespace is the workload's network stack. Under gVisor in sandbox networking mode, the namespace is a plumbing point for frames, and the workload's sockets, routes and ARP state live in the Sentry. Host tools such as ip route and ss therefore show runc workloads accurately but show only the outer edge of a gVisor workload.

Second, checkpointing a runc container means checkpointing host processes from outside. CRIU freezes the processes with the freezer cgroup or ptrace(PTRACE_SEIZE), injects parasite code to dump memory, reads /proc/<pid>/ files and page maps, and restores by recreating the processes, mappings and descriptors with ordinary syscalls. Checkpointing a gVisor sandbox means asking one program to serialize its own data structures. Substrate's design leans on the second model, and Chapter 13 does not attribute CRIU behaviour to it.

Third, who must be trusted with privilege differs. runc needs enough privilege to create namespaces, mount filesystems and set up cgroups, which is why it normally runs as root on the node. Substrate's gVisor worker runs as an unprivileged Pod container with a fixed capability list. workerpool_apply.go explains each entry: SETUID, SETGID and SETFCAP so the gofer can write a full-range identity mapping for its user namespace, SYS_ADMIN for mounts, NET_ADMIN and NET_RAW for actor networking, and DAC_OVERRIDE, FOWNER and CHOWN for rootfs ownership. It omits SYS_PTRACE and SYS_CHROOT because runsc creates an identity-mapped user namespace while directfs is on and networking is not host. The sandbox gets those capabilities inside that namespace, not from the worker.

2.6 Roadmap and engineering improvements

The repository-backed facts in this chapter are narrow but important. Substrate pins runsc flags in internal_flags.json. They include JSON logging, --host-settings=ignore, --cpu-num-from-quota for create and restore, -allow-connected-on-save at start, and -background -detach at restore. It shapes OCI specifications for gVisor in ShapeGVisor and invokes runsc through runsc.go. The worker capability list and its rationale live in the WorkerPool controller. Each of these is a compatibility surface. A runsc upgrade that changes the meaning of a flag, the CRI annotation names or the directfs user-namespace behaviour changes the worker's required privileges or the actor's behaviour.

Proposals follow from that. A conformance suite could assert, per pinned runsc release, the observable facts this book relies on: platform selection, the user-namespace mapping that removes SYS_PTRACE from the worker, the set of checkpoint files, and sandbox-mode networking. A second proposal is to record runsc's version and platform in the actor's runtime information so an operator can correlate behaviour without reading runtime logs. A third is documentation work. A short table in the WorkerPool documentation, mapping each worker capability to the runsc behaviour that needs it, would make capability reviews faster than reading controller comments. These are editorial proposals, not current tracked work.

Source map

  • ShapeGVisor: the CRI sandbox annotations, gVisor mount hints and cgroup leaf names Substrate writes into OCI specifications.
  • runsc.go: every runsc command the gVisor worker executes, and how argument vectors are built.
  • internal_flags.json: the pinned global and per-command runsc flags.
  • workerpool_apply.go: worker capability sets and the gVisor user-namespace rationale.

3. From kubectl apply to a Pod Bound to a Node

This chapter follows a single manifest, pod.yaml, from the operator's terminal to the moment the kubelet on one node decides to run it. It covers kubectl, the API server's request pipeline, etcd, the watch machinery that every controller depends on, the scheduler, and the kubelet's view of its assigned Pods. Chapter 4 continues on the node, from the kubelet's first CRI call to a running process. Chapters 9 and 13 then trace the equivalent journey for an actor, and the comparison tables in Chapter 9 refer back to the sections here.

Everything in this chapter is upstream Kubernetes behaviour. Exact defaults change between releases. The structure described, a central API server persisting to etcd with clients reacting through watches, has been stable for many releases and is what Substrate's own control plane is contrasted with.

3.1 kubectl turns a file into an HTTP request

The example manifest is minimal:

apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: web
  namespace: default
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: registry.example/web:1.0
    ports:
    - containerPort: 8080

kubectl apply -f pod.yaml performs several steps before anything reaches the cluster.

  1. Configuration and credentials. kubectl reads the kubeconfig (~/.kube/config or $KUBECONFIG), selects a context, and obtains the API server URL, the cluster CA bundle and a client credential. That can be a client certificate, a bearer token, or an exec plugin that mints a short-lived token.
  2. Discovery. It fetches the server's API discovery documents (/api, /apis, and the aggregated discovery endpoint in current releases) and caches them under ~/.kube/cache. Discovery maps the manifest's apiVersion and kind to a REST resource, here pods in the core group, and tells kubectl that Pods are namespaced.
  3. Decoding. The YAML is decoded to an unstructured object. Client-side validation is no longer the primary check; current kubectl asks the server to validate fields (fieldValidation=Strict or Warn).
  4. Apply semantics. With the default client-side apply, kubectl GETs the live object. If it does not exist, kubectl sends a POST /api/v1/namespaces/default/pods with the object and an annotation recording the applied configuration. If it exists, kubectl computes a three-way strategic merge patch between the last applied configuration, the live object and the new file, and sends a PATCH. With --server-side, kubectl instead sends a PATCH with content type application/apply-patch+yaml, and the server performs the merge, tracking field ownership in metadata.managedFields.

The transport is HTTPS. kubectl verifies the server certificate against the cluster CA and negotiates HTTP/2 where available. Requests are JSON by default for kubectl. Built-in controllers use the more compact protobuf encoding (application/vnd.kubernetes.protobuf). Every later component in this chapter talks to the API server, and only the API server talks to etcd.

3.2 Inside the API server: authentication to persistence

The kube-apiserver processes every request through a fixed chain of handlers. The order explains many operational behaviours.

Stage What happens Typical failure
TLS and HTTP Terminate TLS, apply request timeouts and max in-flight limits Connection refused, 429
Authentication Client certificate CN/O, bearer token, service account JWT, OIDC or webhook produce a user, groups and extra fields 401 Unauthorized
Audit Record request metadata according to policy None for the client
API Priority and Fairness Classify the request into a flow schema and priority level, queue fairly 429 Too Many Requests
Authorization RBAC, Node authorizer, webhook: may this user create pods in default? 403 Forbidden
Decoding and defaulting Convert to the internal version, apply defaults such as restartPolicy: Always and dnsPolicy: ClusterFirst 400 Bad Request
Mutating admission Built-in plugins (for example ServiceAccount injection, DefaultStorageClass) then mutating webhooks Webhook rejection
Validation Field validation for the object and its subresources 422 Unprocessable Entity
Validating admission Built-in plugins, ValidatingAdmissionPolicy (CEL), validating webhooks, Pod Security admission 403 or 422
Storage Encode as protobuf, write to etcd 409 Conflict, 500

For the example Pod, the ServiceAccount admission plugin sets spec.serviceAccountName: default and adds a projected volume containing a bound service-account token, the cluster CA and the namespace. The API server also fills metadata.uid, metadata.creationTimestamp and the initial status.phase: Pending.

The storage layer writes to etcd through the etcd v3 gRPC API over mutually authenticated TLS. A create is a transaction: if the key /registry/pods/default/web has never been modified, then put the encoded object. An update is guarded by the object's previous modification revision. This compare-and-swap is the source of Kubernetes optimistic concurrency. Every object's metadata.resourceVersion is the etcd revision at which it was last written, and a client update carrying a stale resourceVersion fails with 409 Conflict.

etcd itself replicates the write through Raft. The leader appends the entry to its log, replicates it to followers, and acknowledges once a majority has persisted it, which includes an fdatasync of the write-ahead log on each of those members. Only then does the API server return 201 Created to kubectl. At this point the Pod exists, but nothing has happened on any node.

3.3 Watches, the cacher and informers

Kubernetes components do not poll for new objects. They watch. Understanding the watch path is necessary to answer the question this book keeps asking: who tells whom, and how.

etcd exposes a gRPC Watch stream that delivers every change to a key range after a given revision. The API server opens these streams itself, one per resource type, and feeds them into an in-memory watch cache, the cacher. Clients never watch etcd directly. When a client sends GET /api/v1/pods?watch=1&resourceVersion=N, the API server serves the stream from the cacher. It keeps the HTTP response open and writes one JSON or protobuf frame per event (ADDED, MODIFIED, DELETED, BOOKMARK), using chunked transfer encoding on HTTP/1.1 or a long-lived stream on HTTP/2. Field and label selectors, such as spec.nodeName=node-a, are evaluated in the cacher so each client receives only relevant events.

Client libraries wrap this in the informer pattern from client-go.

  1. A reflector performs ListAndWatch. It lists the resource to obtain the current objects and a collection resourceVersion, then watches from that version. In current releases it can instead request a streaming list, which delivers the initial state as watch events followed by a bookmark.
  2. Events go into a DeltaFIFO, which records sequences of changes per object key.
  3. A shared informer pops deltas, updates a thread-safe indexer (the local cache, with indexes such as by namespace or by node), and invokes registered event handlers.
  4. Controllers' handlers do not do work directly. They enqueue object keys into a rate-limited workqueue, and worker goroutines reconcile each key by reading from the local cache and writing desired changes back through the API server.
  5. If a watch breaks, the reflector resumes from the last seen resourceVersion. If that version has been compacted out of etcd or the cacher (410 Gone), it relists.
  6. Periodic resync redelivers cached objects to handlers so level-based controllers can repair drift without new events.

The important property is that state flows through one place. The scheduler, the kubelet and every controller observe the same object history through the API server, and each writes its decisions back as object updates. No component sends the kubelet an imperative "start this Pod" call. The kubelet discovers that a Pod has been assigned to it by watching.

3.4 The scheduler chooses a node and writes a binding

kube-scheduler runs informers for Pods, Nodes, PersistentVolumes, PersistentVolumeClaims, CSI nodes, storage classes and other objects it needs to evaluate placement. Its Pod informer delivers the new Pod because its spec.nodeName is empty and its spec.schedulerName is default-scheduler.

The Pod enters the scheduling queue. The queue has three parts: an active heap ordered by priority and enqueue time, a backoff queue for Pods that recently failed, and an unschedulable set of Pods that wait for a cluster event, such as a new node or a freed resource, that might make them schedulable. A scheduling cycle pops one Pod and runs the scheduling framework's extension points.

Extension point Purpose Examples
PreEnqueue, QueueSort Gate and order Pods Scheduling gates, priority sort
PreFilter, Filter Remove infeasible nodes NodeResourcesFit, NodeAffinity, TaintToleration, VolumeBinding, PodTopologySpread
PostFilter React when no node fits DefaultPreemption chooses victims to evict
PreScore, Score, NormalizeScore Rank feasible nodes NodeResourcesBalancedAllocation, ImageLocality, InterPodAffinity
Reserve Claim resources in the scheduler's own cache VolumeBinding reserves volumes
Permit Approve, deny or delay Gang scheduling plugins
PreBind, Bind, PostBind Persist the decision VolumeBinding binds claims; DefaultBinder posts the binding

For large clusters, Filter stops after finding enough feasible nodes (percentageOfNodesToScore), so the scheduler does not necessarily evaluate every node. After Score, the scheduler assumes the Pod onto the chosen node in its cache. The next Pod can then be scheduled immediately, with that capacity already consumed, while binding proceeds asynchronously in a separate binding cycle.

Binding is an API write: POST /api/v1/namespaces/default/pods/web/binding with a Binding object naming the target node. The API server's binding subresource sets spec.nodeName on the Pod and records the PodScheduled condition. If binding fails, the scheduler forgets the assumed Pod and requeues it. The scheduler never contacts the node.

3.5 The kubelet learns about its Pod and starts work

Each kubelet runs a Pod config source that watches the API server for Pods with spec.nodeName equal to its node name. Its credentials are restricted by the Node authorizer and the NodeRestriction admission plugin, so it can read only objects related to its own Pods and update only its own Node and Pod statuses. Static Pods from a manifest directory or URL are merged into the same configuration stream.

When the bound Pod arrives, the kubelet's main sync loop dispatches it to a per-Pod pod worker, a goroutine that serializes all lifecycle work for that Pod UID.
