Some comments near the top of the protocol still describe a single guest and microVM as future work. The implementations support both runtimes and multiple hosted actors. Interface review must therefore read message fields and server implementations, not preserve outdated narrative comments as semantics. The actor identity and directories on each request identify the specific workload; a worker-wide available/executing binary state is not an adequate model for current concurrent hosting.

ActorDirs is a concrete part of the boundary. Atelet supplies paths rather than making the worker reconstruct all directories from UID. Checkpoint and restore directories may live on a different filesystem from the actor root, so the worker must not assume cross-directory rename or hard-link operations are possible. Runtime asset paths are constrained to the staged actor asset directory. These rules protect both portability of node storage layout and the integrity of executable assets.

A runtime implementation must cover failure transitions, not only the successful boot path. If network setup succeeds and runtime startup fails, it must close namespace references and listeners. If checkpoint captures memory but filesystem capture fails, it must report failure without advertising a complete snapshot. If restore fails after creating a VMM process, termination must remove it and its mounts. The existing workers' hosted-actor machinery, shutdown paths, crash handling, and root-gated tests are more useful templates than a minimal RunWorkload handler.

Fidelity is a shared semantic contract. VOLUMES, ROOTFS, and MEMORY identify cumulative state preservation levels. A backend may serialize them differently, but it must return and restore what the declared fidelity means. A runtime that can preserve a writable rootfs but not process memory should not label its snapshot MEMORY for API convenience. Runtime version compatibility also matters: saved process state can require the exact runtime assets, while filesystem-only recovery may cold boot under a default runtime with its own compatibility constraints.

Resource requirements reach the worker through the protocol. gVisor and microVM enforce them through different mechanisms, such as cgroup/OCI limits or VM sizing. A new backend must define what its reported usage and admission size mean. A VM's configured memory, host resident memory, shared page cache, and guest-reported memory are not interchangeable. The API's placement accounting relies on declared resource semantics, while observability may report sampled physical usage. An extension must not silently change one into the other.

Statistics methods deliberately avoid blocking behind the lifecycle mutex. GetWorkloadStats distinguishes an actor not hosted here from an actor accepted but not yet measured. GetActiveWorkloadStats returns attribution with each sample, including an unspecified source when measurement is not available. Consumers must attribute from the returned identity rather than a stale worker-to-actor map. A new runtime that blocks its stats handler for the whole restore would hide exactly the resource spike operators need to observe.

The node-to-worker protocol is not a public third-party runtime SDK with a guaranteed independent release cycle at v1.0.0. It is an internal seam designed to support controlled skew. The version-skew policy covers Substrate's own components, built from one commit and upgraded in the documented order. It does not promise compatibility to third-party worker images. The practical path is to integrate and test the backend with a core release and follow the skew rules for that release.

Host-kernel prerequisites belong in the runtime contract

A runtime extension can require KVM, TAP, userfaultfd, namespaces, cgroups, or mount support. Those prerequisites affect the device plugin, WorkerPool rendering, node setup, and CI. They cannot be hidden in an image and discovered only after placement. The current microVM path illustrates this: /dev/kvm availability, asset architecture, virtio-fs, and kernel behavior constrain whether a worker can execute the assigned workload.

The outer worker security context also needs review. Adding a capability or changing seccomp behavior affects the shared infrastructure boundary, not just one application. A backend's own sandbox can fail to initialize if the outer profile rejects required syscalls, but disabling all outer restrictions without understanding the backend is not a compatibility design. The current code makes explicit choices for gVisor and microVM; a new class needs equally explicit rationale and tests.

17.4 Gateway augmentation, policy boundaries, and preview features

Gateway augmentation and gateway replacement have different obligations. An additional egress ext_proc service, enabled with --experimental-additional-egress-extproc-service, runs after Substrate authenticates the actor and applies its EgressPolicy. It receives headers and actor context and can deny or add headers. The current mechanism is experimental and header-only. It does not receive arbitrary body content merely because Envoy's general ext_proc API can support body processing.

A service using this extension must preserve the trust of the actor metadata it receives. The metadata is meaningful because the preceding gateway path authenticated it. If the extension is reachable independently, it must authenticate its callers or otherwise constrain access. It should also define failure behavior: a policy enforcement point that becomes unavailable must not silently turn a required inspection into permission. The installer and dataplane configuration determine the actual callout behavior, so review the rendered filter chain as well as the service implementation.

Replacing the egress gateway transfers more responsibility. The replacement must validate actor certificates and attribute traffic to an actor in an appropriate current state. The network egress contract describes the tunnel protocol and identity expectations. It is encouraged to honor Substrate EgressPolicy, but a custom PEP may use its own policy system. Operators must know which policy is authoritative; leaving an EgressPolicy object in the API while the replacement ignores it can create a false sense of enforcement.

Ingress replacement is broader still. The router does more than inspect requests: it parses actor targets, resumes suspended actors, handles overload, resolves assignment, and routes with the correct worker identity. The security extensibility document marks generalized ingress augmentation and replacement as planned. AgentGateway is a concrete alternate dataplane integration, but it is not evidence that every arbitrary gateway can be substituted without implementing the same lifecycle and identity behavior.

The extension must preserve the distinction between caller identity and actor identity. An upstream human-facing gateway authenticates a user and chooses an actor. Substrate's ingress allowlist trusts that gateway as a component; it does not currently enforce per-actor user grants. A vendor adding richer ingress policy needs a defined representation for the original caller, a trustworthy propagation path, and a decision before activation if unauthorized requests must not consume restore capacity. That is a new authorization contract, not just another header.

Preview gates provide a mechanism for exposing incomplete capabilities deliberately. internal/preview currently lists ExternalVolumes, GoldenEgressPolicy, and PerTemplateSnapshotLocation. Gates are process-wide, but user requests must also opt in through a metadata header. kubectl ate --preview supplies that opt-in. Substrate components use dial options that opt in for system work so they can maintain and clean up enabled resources.

Declarative validation connects gates to API fields. Proto comments carry preview documentation and Kubernetes validation tags; generated Go validation evaluates the operation context. The guide requires wrappers to build create/update operations through the preview-aware helpers. A bare operation value could omit gate state and defeat the intended field restriction. This is why adding a comment alone does not implement a gate: the generated validation and its call site must both participate.

Cleanup paths should remain available when a gate is turned off. Gating server-written status or every system operation can strand resources created while the feature was enabled. The workflow entry points explicitly opt into system work, and tests enforce that pattern. A preview feature needs a disablement story as much as an enablement story. For an external volume, for example, refusing a new attachment is compatible with continuing to detach an existing one.

Preview is not equivalent to version negotiation. It expresses operator and client consent to use a feature in the current implementation. It does not prove an older worker understands a newly added field, and it does not override the component skew rules. A release can enable a gate on the API while still needing workers upgraded first. The compatibility review must consider both dimensions independently.

Testing must include gates off and on, and requests with and without opt-in. The CI matrix does this for end-to-end lanes. A feature test that skips when its gate is disabled is appropriate only if another lane deliberately enables it and the test runner proves that lane ran. The repository's fail-closed CI conventions exist to prevent a configuration mistake from turning every test into a successful skip.

17.5 Compatibility across RPCs, database state, node files, and snapshots

Compatibility is not one binary property. The version-skew policy defines a directed order: certificate controller, atelet, workers, API server, Kubernetes controller, networking, then clients. A component can be one compatible release ahead of components later in that order, but not ahead of dependencies earlier in it. API and IDP move together. Within a rollout, replicas of one component can be split across two adjacent releases.

That order creates specific message directions. A new atelet can drive old workers and call an old API. An old controller can render Pods for new workers. Old clients can call a new API. The reverse combinations are not all supported. These facts determine when a caller may begin sending a new field and whether a new worker can assume a new Pod template. A final-state compatibility test does not cover the mixed state that exists during a rollout.

The worker Pod template is particularly restrictive. From v1.0, the policy requires the same template for the same WorkerPool within a major release, so upgrading the controller after workers does not unexpectedly roll them again. New behavior must arrive through the image or an explicit new WorkerPool field, and new workers must accept the flags and environment produced by the old controller. An apparently harmless default flag change can therefore violate the rollout contract even if the new controller and worker agree with each other.

Unknown protobuf fields have deliberately different handling by role. API servers reject unknown request fields, preventing a client from assuming a field was honored when it was ignored. When reading stored objects written by a newer replica, an older API server drops fields it cannot validate and serves the reduced object. Read-modify-write clients preserve unknown fields so an old client does not erase fields the server still understands. The CLI rejects unknown manifest fields. These choices are contextual rather than a universal rule to always keep or always discard unknown data.

Atelet and workers reject fields they do not know. Because a newer atelet can call an older worker, introducing an internal request field requires two releases: the worker learns to accept it first; the caller begins sending it in a later minor release. This is compatibility through staged behavior, not through silently accepting arbitrary fields. Patch releases cannot carry such staged additions, because an upgrade can skip patch releases and a rollback can land on any of them.

CRD changes have their own timing. New CRDs are applied with the controller, after components such as atelet have already upgraded. Those components must therefore work against the old CRD shape until that step. Compatible changes add optional fields; the served CRD version has no conversion machinery that magically preserves every removed field during rollback. Reapplying old schemas can prune fields unknown to the old version, and users must stop using new fields when rolling back.

Database migrations are shared across replicas. The first new API instance can apply a migration while old instances still serve. postgresql-schema-evolution.md requires every committed migration prefix to remain readable and writable by the previous binary. A sequence that becomes compatible only after its final migration is unsafe because a failure can leave the database at any intermediate prefix. Goose's per-migration commits make those boundaries durable states.

The expand-and-contract pattern therefore spans releases. Add the new structure while preserving old behavior, transition readers and writers while keeping both representations consistent, and remove the old structure only after the supported previous binary no longer needs it. New columns need compatible nullability or defaults. New constraints must allow values an old binary can still write. Large backfills do not belong in startup migrations that hold readiness hostage. There are no down migrations in the contract; binary rollback retains the newer schema.

Node files are another protocol. Atelet and workers share directories, sockets, and selected files such as runtime metadata. Their layout must remain readable in both upgrade and rollback directions within supported skew. A layout change can require a first release that reads old and new forms while writing the old form, followed by a later release that writes the new form. Renaming an internal directory is not merely a refactor when another process or an older binary can still hold a path to it.

Snapshot manifests live longer than node-local coordination files. Within a major, a release must read earlier snapshots, and new manifest fields must be safe for older readers to ignore on rollback. The runtime's own checkpoint representation follows separate rules. A runsc memory image or hypervisor state cannot be assumed portable simply because the Substrate manifest parses. SandboxConfig records available runtime versions so memory restore can select the version that produced the state.

Filesystem-only recovery has its own caveats. MicroVM rootfs and durable-directory archives are Substrate-managed representations. gVisor uses fscheckpoint bundles written by runsc. The version-skew policy explicitly notes that Substrate does not prove a new default runsc can read every bundle an older version wrote; a failure can crash the actor. “Files survive runtime replacement” is an intended recovery path with a concrete compatibility dependency, not an unconditional theorem.

Reviewing one change across all domains

Suppose a new runtime option affects checkpoint compression and adds a request field, a manifest field, and a SandboxConfig asset. The request field needs caller/callee skew staging. The manifest field must be safe for older readers. The runtime asset must remain fetchable for saved memory state. The controller must render a compatible worker envelope. The object-store plugin must still preserve exact bytes and commit ordering. Tests need old/new combinations and rollback, not just a new-version round trip.

Now suppose the change is only a credential-provider URI extension. It may avoid core database changes, but it still affects parser validation, authorization, error handling, secret redaction, and old plugin behavior. If the gateway begins emitting the new URI while an older provider remains deployed, the provider should reject it clearly rather than interpret it as a different secret. The rollout order and feature enablement must be documented even when protobuf wire fields do not change.

This is the practical value of an explicit boundary map. It lets a reviewer enumerate which readers and writers persist beyond the current process lifetime. Compatibility defects often arise from a reader the author forgot: an old CLI, a draining worker, a stored tag, an earlier API replica, or a node directory reused after restart. The schema compiler cannot find all of those relationships; the architecture and tests must make them visible.

A mixed-version exercise should preserve objects written at each stage of the rollout, not only test the final pair of binaries. For example, retain a snapshot from before the upgrade, one written while API replicas are mixed, and one written after completion, then perform the supported rollback and attempt the documented recovery paths. Keep node files produced by the newer supervisor when restarting the older supported supervisor. This exposes compatibility obligations that a clean reinstall erases. A test environment rebuilt from scratch for every binary combination cannot demonstrate that persisted state survives those transitions.

The same discipline applies to generated clients. A read-modify-write test should retain a field unknown to the older client when the newer server still accepts it. A create test using that unknown field against an older server should be rejected according to the policy. Those outcomes can appear contradictory until their ownership is explicit: the client preserves data it does not own, while the server refuses new requests it cannot validate. Testing both directions prevents an apparently helpful normalizer from stripping newer state during routine updates.

17.6 Roadmap and engineering improvements

The repository's documented extension roadmap includes generalized ingress augmentation and replacement, a fuller egress replacement path than the partial one the extensibility guide describes, and additional backend plugins outside core. Runtime independence is a design objective reflected in the atelet-worker boundary and future skew policy. It is not yet a universal promise that arbitrary worker releases or external runtimes can mix with any API version.

Several architectural targets remain broader than current extension contracts. Actor-to-actor routing needs addressing, activation, and authorization semantics. More advanced memory storage or incremental snapshots need clear ownership of bytes, dirty-state tracking, commit, and recovery. Current microVM sparse-delta merging produces complete snapshots for the applicable restore mode; it is not a generic object-store chain of incremental snapshots. An extension claiming incremental persistence must define how chains are retained, compacted, authorized, and recovered after partial failure.

The current default microVM memory-restore choice also constrains future runtime work. Cloud Hypervisor version and prefault behavior determine whether the worker uses eager copy or on-demand handling. A new backend or optimized path must expose measured behavior rather than assuming userfaultfd always reduces end-to-end latency. Demand paging moves work after initial restore and can increase later fault latency; the correct objective is application readiness and useful work under the expected access pattern.

Editorial proposals include reusable conformance suites for public plugins, explicit mixed-version integration tests, and contract documentation generated alongside protobufs. A credential suite can verify caller trust, URI rejection, denial semantics, redaction, and backend outage behavior. An object-store suite can verify byte fidelity, manifest-last ordering, idempotent retry, copy, cleanup, and asset isolation. A runtime suite can verify attribution, cleanup after each failure point, resource limits, fidelity, and network activation ordering.

A second proposal is to require each new extension point to state its authority and cancellation model before implementation. The statement should answer who may call it, what identity is attested, what success commits, what partial work may remain, and what a retry does. This small amount of design information is more valuable than a generic interface that leaves every implementer to invent those answers. Existing object-store comments show how much correctness can be captured directly at the protocol boundary.

Finally, compatibility evidence should become an artifact of a release. The version-skew policy defines the intended combinations; tests should demonstrate them with the old and new binaries, database schema prefixes, node files, and representative snapshots. The release can then distinguish tested compatibility from a plausible design. Until that evidence exists for a particular pair, operators and extension authors should follow the stated support boundary and avoid treating a successful same-version test as proof of upgrade safety.

Source map

  • Code layout, public control API, credential API, and object-store API: supported external seams.
  • Object-store plugin command, storage configuration, S3 uploader, and microVM asset staging: backend integration and RustFS reuse.
  • Worker protocol, shared node paths, gVisor worker, and microVM worker: internal runtime contract.
  • Gateway extension guide, egress contract, preview mechanism, and preview guide: policy integration and controlled feature exposure.
  • Version-skew policy, database evolution, API validation, and integration repository conventions: evolution across releases and repositories.

Appendix A. Linux Primitive and Kernel-Interface Audit

This audit distinguishes a syscall issued by Substrate from a kernel mechanism reached through a library or an external runtime. Direct means first-party code invokes the Linux interface or writes its control filesystem. Library means a checked wrapper performs the syscall. Runtime means runsc, Cloud Hypervisor, virtiofsd, the outer container runtime, or a CSI driver owns the operation. Tooling marks benchmark/test behavior rather than production execution.

The source column gives exact paths in the audited clone. A source file for a runtime-mediated mechanism is the Substrate integration point, not a claim that the external runtime's implementation is vendored there. Ordinary Go file and network operations also use Linux syscalls; the table groups those by their architectural role instead of pretending that a static inventory determines every syscall a compiled binary will issue.

Linux Primitive / Syscall / Kernel Mechanism Substrate Package & File Kernel-Level Function Substrate Purpose
Process creation and execve through os/exec — library cmd/ateworker-gvisor/runsc.go; cmd/ateworker-microvm/internal/ch/restorefds.go Creates a process and replaces its image while arranging inherited descriptors and process attributes. Starts sandbox helpers independently of the worker Pod's lifecycle; runtime exit and RPC completion remain separate events.
runsc checkpoint, fscheckpoint, and restore -background -detach — runtime API cmd/ateworker-gvisor/runsc.go; cmd/ateworker-gvisor/fscheckpoint.go These are userspace runtime commands, not Linux syscalls. The host supplies memory, process, and file services while runsc serializes its own kernel state. Captures process, filesystem, and rootfs state at different fidelities. Restore-completion waits control when backing snapshot files can be reclaimed.
prctl(PR_SCHED_CORE, PR_SCHED_CORE_GET) — direct cmd/ateworker-gvisor/main.go Queries support for Linux core scheduling. Allows the runsc wrapper to enable core tags when the host supports them; this is distinct from ordinary CPU quotas.
cgroup v2 mount/delegation, cgroup.procs, cgroup.subtree_control — direct internal/ateworker/cgroup/cgroup.go Builds a controller hierarchy under the container's delegated cgroup namespace and moves processes into leaves. Gives each concurrently hosted actor an accounting domain while checking that setup is not manipulating the host cgroup root.
cpu.max, memory.high, memory.max, memory.current, memory.stat — direct/runtime internal/ateworker/cgroup/actor.go; internal/ocispec/gvisor.go Enforces CPU bandwidth, memory throttling or hard limits, and usage accounting. Separates admission bookings from host enforcement. Actor memory throttling, Pod limits, guest limits, and Sentry-reported memory have different scopes.
PSI memory.pressure and memory.events.local — direct internal/ateworker/cgroup/memwatch.go Reports time stalled on memory pressure and cgroup-local memory events. Distinguishes a persistently stuck actor from transient allocation activity before the guard intervenes.
cgroup.kill and cgroup.events — direct internal/ateworker/cgroup/memguard.go; internal/ateworker/cgroup/actor.go Kills the processes in a cgroup and exposes whether it remains populated. Reclaims an offending actor without intentionally invoking the worker Pod's kernel OOM path. Successful request submission is not the same as completed teardown.
clone3(CLONE_INTO_CGROUP) through Go UseCgroupFD — library internal/ateworker/cgroup/actor.go Places a new child into the selected cgroup as part of creation. Starts actor host processes in the correct accounting domain. Substrate sets SysProcAttr; the Go runtime owns the syscall implementation.
Checkpoint page-cache charging and temporary memory borrowing — direct cmd/ateworker-gvisor/ckptcgroup.go; internal/ateworker/memborrow/memborrow.go File-cache pages consume cgroup memory; memory.high can reclaim and throttle writers. Moves the Sentry into a checkpoint sibling and lends unused worker memory to checkpoint work without silently promising the same memory to another actor.
prctl(PR_SET_CHILD_SUBREAPER), wait4(WNOHANG), process signals — direct internal/ateworker/pid1/pid1.go Reparents orphaned descendants, collects exits, and delivers termination requests. Prevents zombie accumulation and preserves worker shutdown semantics when runtime helpers create descendants.
pidfd_open, pidfd_send_signal, poll, descriptor duplication — direct internal/pidfd/pidfd.go; cmd/ateworker-gvisor/sandboxexit.go Supplies a stable process reference, exit readiness, and signaling without relying only on a reusable PID. Tracks sandbox death and avoids signaling an unrelated process after PID reuse.

Keeps actor network identity separate from the worker Pod. Thread locking and restoration are required because namespace membership is an OS-thread property.

Forces allowed TCP traffic through atunnel and blocks bypass paths. This implementation uses REDIRECT, not TPROXY.
getsockopt(SO_ORIGINAL_DST) and IPv6 equivalent — direct internal/linuxsys/original_dst_linux.go Retrieves the destination tuple recorded before NAT redirection. Recovers the actor's intended egress endpoint for proxy routing and policy enforcement.

Provides the microVM hardware boundary. The device plugin arranges access; Cloud Hypervisor issues the KVM ioctls.

Implements the optional OnDemand restore path. The baseline's default Cloud Hypervisor v53.0 selects eager Copy instead because the version policy treats its prefault behavior as unsuitable.

Serializes test resources, generates controlled CPU work, and measures tunnel benchmarks. These uses must not be confused with production actor scheduling.

Reading the indirect mechanisms correctly

The Linux kernel's userfaultfd documentation defines fault notification and userspace fault resolution. Substrate selects a Cloud Hypervisor restore mode; it does not implement a Go userfaultfd handler. The KVM API documentation defines the descriptor/ioctl model used by the VMM. A device-plugin allocation establishes permission to reach that model; it does not itself create a VM.

The cgroup v2 documentation defines hierarchical accounting and control. Substrate layers resource bookings, actor leaves, checkpoint borrowing, and pressure observation above those mechanisms. None of those userspace decisions converts memory.high into an unconditional hard allocation limit.

gVisor's architecture introduction and security model explain the userspace-kernel boundary. The exact platform-specific trap, memory and syscall behavior belongs to the pinned runsc build and its flags. Similarly, Envoy's event loops, TLS library behavior, and dynamic-module execution depend on its compiled artifact. This appendix does not infer a complete transitive syscall trace from their presence in the deployment.

What this audit does not equate

PostgreSQL row locks, SQL leases, OpenFGA relations, gRPC, TLS, SPIFFE, and CSI are not Linux primitives. They rely on operating-system services but define different consistency or authorization contracts. Keeping them outside the syscall classification prevents a common error: attributing an application-level guarantee to the kernel mechanism that merely carries its messages.

A complete runtime trace would need the exact binary hashes, architecture, host kernel and configuration, container runtime, workload, and restore path. It would also need scenarios beyond successful startup: canceled restoration, socket replacement, filesystem fallback, OOM pressure, worker restart, and node loss. The static audit identifies where to instrument those scenarios and which claims require that evidence; it does not replace it.

Kubernetes infrastructure API api/infra/k8s/ate/v1 kube-apiserver, controllers, supervisor, generated clientset/listers/informers.
WorkerSupport and Atelet internal/proto/ateletpb/atelet.proto Worker-to-node support and API-to-node execution coordination.
Worker execution API internal/proto/ateworkerpb/ateworker.proto Node supervisor and both worker backends.

Credential provider api/credprovider/v1/credprovider.proto Egress gateway and credential backend.

pkg/client is the generated Kubernetes infrastructure client. The actor API client comes from the generated bindings next to api/ateapi/v1/ateapi.proto. Confusing the two leads to incorrect assumptions about watches, resource versions, authentication, and persistence.

Implementation, target, and unfinished work

Topic Status at v1.0.0 Evidence and interpretation
Multiple active actors per worker Implemented Scheduler bookings and both runtime admission paths account for slots, CPU and memory.
Automatic idle suspension Not wired into production workers suspend requester and upward RPCs exist, but no production runtime constructs the requester; parking demo explicitly describes the missing automation.
Activation latency Target, not demonstrated by this audit architecture sets 100ms at p95. Runtime timings alone omit storage, admission, routing, and probes.
Billion actors and 1,000 wakeups/s North-star targets The same architecture document names them; they are not acceptance-test results in this manuscript.
MicroVM demand paging Implemented conditionally, not the default staged behavior prefault policy, restore selection, and asset pins lead to Copy for the default CH v53.0.
Incremental snapshot mechanics Partial implementation sparse merge completes OnDemand deltas. It does not implement remote incremental snapshot chains.
Tiered state storage Concrete local/durable paths; no general page-tiering contract snapshot tracker and caches distinguish node-local files and object storage. Host page cache is another resource domain, not proof of a policy-controlled RAM/SSD/object-page hierarchy.
Runtime-aware restore and fidelity fallback Implemented Scheduler/runtime metadata and resume workflows preserve sandbox class while selecting compatible memory restore or a permitted lower fidelity.
Actor-to-actor authorization Future security status marks it future; default lateral network access is blocked.
Per-actor ingress authorization Absent Static SPIFFE client allowlisting does not grant only selected actor targets.
External volumes Preview preview gates gate CSI-backed external volumes. Actor cloning with those volumes is constrained by missing CSI snapshot integration.
Per-template storage locations and golden egress policy Preview Both are explicit gates in the same source.
GCS actor-scoped transfer credentials Implemented objectstore-plugin README and exchange implementation scope transfers by actor.
S3/RustFS actor-scoped transfer credentials Not implemented in the in-tree S3 path S3 uses the plugin's configured ambient credentials; supporting S3 does not imply parity with GCS credential exchange.
Egress additional ext_proc Experimental, headers-only extensibility guide describes the current hook, enabled by --experimental-additional-egress-extproc-service, after built-in checks.
Ingress augmentation/replacement Documented future work The same guide names planned work; existing alternate AgentGateway wiring should be discussed separately.
Version-skew contract Applies from 1.0.0 version-skew policy defines supported skew and upgrade order for compatible releases; the README states the compatibility commitment.
Actor-level telemetry correlation Incomplete observability guide and metrics gaps enumerate missing attribution and instrumentation.

Evidence from tests and benchmarks

The repository's CI runs ordinary/race tests, Rust-module checks, privileged Linux tests, and a runtime/dataplane/preview matrix. AgentGateway's lane has different gating semantics from the principal lane. The workflow is evidence of intended validation coverage, not evidence that this checkout passed that coverage while the book was written.

The tunnel harness exercises real atunnel and namespace behavior while replacing other components. The Nighthawk ingress harness uses an adaptive mean-plus-two-standard-deviations criterion that must not be relabeled as p95. Phase analysis joins node and runtime records; overlapping phases cannot simply be added. These distinctions determine which production claims a measurement can support.

Runtime provenance

The gVisor SandboxConfig default version v7 pins release 20261102.0, and version v6 (20261026.0) stays enabled for memory snapshots taken on it. Each has per-architecture digests. The installer microVM asset code defaults to Kata 4.3.1 and Cloud Hypervisor v53.0. The copied Kata message definitions document their own upstream provenance and compatibility check; they are not a vendored full Kata runtime.

RustFS is pinned to 1.0.3 by digest in the local manifest. The exact storage semantics relevant to Substrate include object writes, reads and ranges, prefix copy/delete, multipart behavior, error handling, and restart persistence. A successful bucket creation proves only one small part of that contract. The book treats the repository integration as evidence of the chosen backend path and calls for workload-specific validation before assigning a production durability objective to it.

Appendix C. Glossary and Reading Paths

Terms here follow the v1.0.0 implementation. Capitalized resource names identify concrete API or Kubernetes types; lower-case process names identify implementations or deployment roles.

Term Meaning and boundary Read next
Actor Logical workload identity and lifecycle record in Substrate's API store. It can exist without an active sandbox. Chapters 1, 5 and 6
ActorAssignment Capacity claim relating an actor to a worker, with identity/incarnation information needed by admission and recovery. Chapter 6
ActorTemplate Immutable client-facing workload definition stored through the Substrate API. Changing an actor's template reference is different from modifying the template. Chapters 5, 12
Atespace Substrate workload/authorization scope. It is not a Kubernetes namespace alias, even when operators use similar names. Chapters 5, 15
Worker API record representing a worker Pod and the execution capacity it advertises. Several actors may be active on it. Chapters 1, 6
WorkerPool Kubernetes CRD that controls a worker fleet and its sandbox-class/configuration selection. Chapters 5, 7
SandboxConfig Cluster-scoped CRD containing runtime versions and digest-addressed assets for a sandbox class. Chapters 5, 8, 17
CSIDriverConfig Cluster-scoped configuration connecting Substrate volume handling to a CSI implementation. Chapters 5, 8, 12
ateapi / ate-api-server Go command and deployment role implementing the actor control plane, PostgreSQL workflows, scheduling and associated controllers. Chapter 6
atecontroller Kubernetes infrastructure reconciliation and Pod-to-Worker synchronization process. Chapter 7
atelet Node supervisor that prepares local state and invokes the worker protocol, with support and storage coordination services. Chapter 8
ateworker A runtime-specific worker process implementing Run/Checkpoint/Restore/Terminate and statistics. The v1.0.0 revision has gVisor and microVM implementations. Chapters 8, 10 and 11
atenet-router Ingress deployment role that resolves actor destinations and triggers resume, using the selected dataplane. Chapter 14
atenet-egress Shared outbound gateway role performing identity, policy and credential handling outside actor sandboxes. Chapters 14 and 15
atunnel Library embedded in the worker for per-actor ingress/egress transport and DNS behavior. Chapter 14
Lease Renewable SQL ownership record used to serialize a workflow. It is not interchangeable with a row lock, assignment uniqueness, or worker epoch. Chapter 6
Worker epoch Worker process incarnation used to reject/reconcile stale work across restarts. Chapters 6, 8
Authoritative admission Capacity revalidation and booking inside the store transaction. Candidate selection alone is advisory. Chapter 6
Golden snapshot Prepared starting state associated with a template's golden workflow, when configured. It is not implied for every possible cold start. Chapters 6, 12
Tag A named retention/reference construct backed by its own copied external snapshot, with sharing and lifecycle semantics. Chapters 5, 12, 15
Fidelity The state layers retained by a snapshot: VOLUMES, ROOTFS, or MEMORY. Chapter 12
VOLUMES Snapshot fidelity retaining DurableDir contents, without promising process-memory continuation or all rootfs writes. Chapter 12
ROOTFS Fidelity adding container writable-rootfs state to the durable-directory layer; processes cold-boot on restore. Chapters 10, 11 and 12
MEMORY Fidelity adding the execution image. It carries runtime compatibility constraints beyond filesystem recovery. Chapters 10, 11 and 12
Locality Retained node-local state that can constrain placement and avoid remote transfer. It is not itself an object-store durability guarantee. Chapters 6, 12
Durable snapshot Completed external snapshot state tracked by the control plane, whose physical resilience depends on the configured storage backend. Chapter 12
Detach Locality-release operation that may require upload before removing a local copy and allowing placement elsewhere. Chapter 12
Revert Lifecycle operation returning an actor to its completed durable state while discarding current execution/local progress as defined by the workflow. Chapters 6, 12
OnDemand Cloud Hypervisor restore mode that faults memory pages as needed. It is conditional in this revision and not the default staged CH v53 path. Chapter 11
Copy Eager guest-memory restoration mode selected by the current version policy for affected or unknown CH versions. Chapter 11
Sentry gVisor userspace kernel hosting the actor's application execution abstraction. It is distinct from host Linux. Chapter 10
virtiofsd Host process serving a filesystem tree to the guest over virtio-fs. Its memory and permissions are part of the microVM boundary. Chapter 11
Runtime asset cache Node-local immutable binary/kernel/image cache, pinned by workers and actors according to use. Chapter 8
Snapshot file cache Cache for shared restore files. Its identity, mutability and eviction rules differ from runtime assets and OCI layers. Chapter 12
RustFS Existing S3-compatible alternative object-store deployment in the kind manifests. Its backend credentials and failure domains remain explicit operational concerns. Chapters 12, 16
Request parking Bounded retention/retry of requests through eligible transient resume failures, with per-actor flight sharing. Chapter 14
SPIFFE identity URI-based workload identity carried in certificates and used by specific authentication/authorization checks. It is not by itself an authorization policy. Chapter 15
Actor JWT Signed token asserting an actor or worker-for-actor role. Relying parties verify it through the issuer's OpenID Connect discovery document and the key set, which lists every key in the signing pool. Chapter 15
EgressPolicy Actor-related outbound policy evaluated outside the sandbox, including permitted requests and credential effects. Chapter 15
AccessPolicy Substrate API authorization configuration using global/atespace scopes and the embedded relation model. Chapter 15
ext_proc Envoy's external processing protocol. The operation being delegated and trusted metadata available depend on the filter chain. Chapters 14 and 15
Preview gate Explicit opt-in for behavior whose availability should not be inferred merely from a schema field or implementation package. Chapters 5, 17
CRI Container Runtime Interface: the gRPC protocol the kubelet speaks over a Unix socket to containerd for sandboxes, containers and images. Actors do not use it. Chapters 2, 3
OCI bundle A directory with config.json and a root filesystem, consumed by an OCI runtime such as runc or runsc. Substrate's worker writes bundles for actors itself. Chapters 2, 9
Runtime shim Long-lived parent of a Pod's container processes, started by containerd and driving runc or runsc. Substrate's PID 1 shim plays a similar role inside the worker. Chapters 2, 4
Pause container Minimal process that pins a Pod's shared namespaces and reaps zombies. Actors have no pause container; named namespace bind mounts pin their network namespaces. Chapter 4
CNI Container Network Interface: plugins executed by containerd that give a Pod's network namespace an interface, IP and routes. The worker programs actor networking itself. Chapters 4, 9
Gofer gVisor helper process that opens host files for the Sentry and serves mounts, in an identity-mapped user namespace under Substrate's flags. Chapters 2, 10
Systrap gVisor platform that traps application system calls with seccomp SECCOMP_RET_TRAP in stub processes and hands them to the Sentry. Chapters 2, 4
Golden snapshot A template's application booted once and captured, so actors created from the template restore it instead of cold-starting. Chapters 7, 9

Follow a problem through the book

A resume is slow. Start with Chapter 16's end-to-end measurement boundary. Use Chapter 14 to distinguish parking and proxy work, Chapter 6 for admission/lease/store contention, Chapter 12 for locality and download, and Chapter 10 or 11 for the actual restore and readiness path. A runtime phase measurement cannot explain an earlier wait for capacity.

A worker restarts while hosting actors. Read Chapter 8's process/registration lifecycle, then Chapter 6's epoch and assignment reconciliation. Chapter 12 explains which local and external snapshot states remain usable. The existence of a checkpoint file is not sufficient evidence that the corresponding actor record should advertise it as durable.

Memory use grows after many restores. Separate actor bookings from host charges using Chapter 8. Read the backend-specific cgroup and memory discussion in Chapter 10 or 11, then snapshot cache/writeback behavior in Chapter 12. Include virtiofsd, host page cache, upload buffers, and concurrent checkpoint loans before concluding that the application leaked memory.

An actor can reach an unexpected endpoint. Follow the network namespace and NAT path in Chapter 14, then identity/policy/DNS and TLS interception in Chapter 15. Inspect the rendered dataplane configuration and active policy cache rather than reasoning from a single base manifest. An ingress allowlist and an egress allow rule protect different traffic directions.

A RustFS deployment is unavailable. Chapter 12 identifies node/control plugin operations that need it and what local locality can still satisfy. Chapter 16 treats object-store recovery, bucket access, credentials, endpoints, PVC persistence and shared infrastructure failure domains. A cache hit may conceal an outage for one actor while another actor cannot resume.

A new runtime version is introduced. Start with Chapter 17's compatibility contract and Chapter 7's SandboxConfig selection/protection. Chapter 8 explains asset publication and worker advertisement. Chapter 6 determines compatible placement; Chapters 10, 11 and 12 determine which state can be reused or downgraded. A new worker image and a new sandbox binary are separate rollout events.

Appendix D. Linux Commands and System Calls, Explained

This appendix gives a short explanation of every Linux command and system call that appears in Chapters 2, 3, 4, 9 and 13. It also says who invokes each one on the Pod path and on the actor path. Pod means the ordinary Kubernetes path through the kubelet, containerd, CNI and runc. Actor means Substrate's path through atelet, the worker and runsc. Where an entry says "runsc", the pinned gVisor runtime performs it on Substrate's behalf, and the exact sequence belongs to that release. Appendix A audits Substrate's kernel interfaces by source file; this appendix is organized by primitive, for readers who want to know what each name means.

Namespaces and process creation

clone / clone3 create a new process or thread. Flags decide what the child shares with its parent and which new namespaces it gets: CLONE_NEWNS (mount), CLONE_NEWPID, CLONE_NEWNET, CLONE_NEWUTS, CLONE_NEWIPC, CLONE_NEWUSER and CLONE_NEWCGROUP. clone3 can also place the child directly into a cgroup with CLONE_INTO_CGROUP and return a pidfd. Pod: runc's nsexec and Go runtime use it to create runc init and the container's PID 1. Actor: runsc uses it to create the Sentry, gofer and stub processes in new namespaces; the worker uses it, through Go's os/exec, to run runsc.

unshare (system call) moves the calling thread or process into new namespaces without creating a child. For a PID namespace it affects only future children. Pod: containerd calls unshare(CLONE_NEWNET) on a locked thread to create a Pod's network namespace, and runc's nsexec uses it for the container's namespaces. Actor: the worker's netns.go uses it to create each actor's runtime and gateway network namespaces.

unshare (command) is the util-linux command that runs a program in new namespaces, for example unshare --net --mount --pid --fork bash. It is a manual tool for experimenting with what runc and runsc automate; neither path runs the command.

setns moves the calling thread into an existing namespace given a file descriptor, from /proc/<pid>/ns/<type> or a bind-mounted namespace file. Mount and user namespaces require a single-threaded caller. Pod: runc's nsexec joins the pause container's network, IPC and UTS namespaces; CNI plugins enter the Pod namespace to configure eth0. Actor: the worker enters actor namespaces on locked OS threads to program interfaces and create namespace-bound sockets.

nsenter is the command-line wrapper around setns: nsenter --target <pid> --net ip addr runs ip addr inside the network namespace of <pid>. It is an operator tool. The lifecycle experiment's collectors use it with --net=<path> to inspect actor namespaces.

ip netns manages named network namespaces. ip netns add x performs unshare(CLONE_NEWNET) and bind-mounts the namespace onto /run/netns/x so it persists without a process; ip netns exec x cmd performs setns and runs a command. containerd and Substrate's worker implement the same technique in Go, so their namespaces appear as files under /var/run/netns (Pods, node view) or /run/netns inside the worker's mount namespace (actors).

Namespace files and bind mounts. Every namespace is visible as a magic link under /proc/<pid>/ns/. Bind-mounting it to an ordinary file keeps the namespace alive after all member processes exit, because the mount holds a reference. Removing the mount (umount) and closing all descriptors destroys it. This is how both containerd and the worker give network namespaces lifetimes independent of processes.

PID namespace. A process tree with its own PID numbering; the first process is PID 1, receives orphans and must reap them, and its exit kills the namespace. Pod: each container normally has its own, or the Pod shares pause's when shareProcessNamespace is set. Actor: runsc puts the Sentry in its own PID namespace on the host; the application's PIDs exist only inside the Sentry.

Mount namespace. A private copy of the mount table, so mounts made inside are invisible outside, subject to propagation settings. Each runc container and each runsc process gets one. The worker's own mount namespace is where actor network namespace files and bundle mounts live, which is why operators reach them through /proc/<worker-pid>/root/.

UTS and IPC namespaces isolate hostname/domainname and System V IPC plus POSIX message queues. Pod containers share pause's, which is why containers in a Pod see the same hostname.

User namespace maps user and group IDs. A process can be root with full capabilities inside while unprivileged outside. Writing uid_map/gid_map that maps ID 0 requires CAP_SETFCAP in the parent namespace since Linux 5.12. Actor: runsc places the gofer and systrap processes in an identity-mapped user namespace when directfs is on, which is why the worker Pod needs SETUID, SETGID and SETFCAP but not SYS_PTRACE or SYS_CHROOT.

cgroup namespace virtualizes the view of /proc/self/cgroup and the cgroup filesystem root, so a container sees its own cgroup as /. This explains why /sys/fs/cgroup inside the worker is not the node's cgroup root.

Filesystems and mounts

mount attaches a filesystem or bind-mounts a directory. Flags such as MS_BIND, MS_REC, MS_RDONLY and MS_REMOUNT, and the propagation flags MS_PRIVATE, MS_SLAVE and MS_SHARED, select the operation. Pod: the kubelet mounts tmpfs for projected volumes, the shim mounts the overlay rootfs, and runc mounts proc, sysfs, /dev and volumes. Actor: the worker bind-mounts namespace files and prepared paths, and runsc's gofer sets up the container filesystem view.

Mount propagation. Shared mounts replicate mount events to peers, slave mounts receive but do not send, and private mounts do neither. runc makes the container root private or slave (mount --make-rprivate /) so container mounts never leak into the host.

umount2 detaches a mount; with MNT_DETACH it is lazy, removing the mount from the namespace immediately and finishing when it is no longer busy. runc detaches the old root after pivot_root. Substrate's image cache detaches actor bundle mounts before deleting directories (mountinfo.go).

pivot_root swaps the process's root mount with another mount point and moves the old root beneath it. Unlike chroot, it changes the mount namespace's root, so the old root can be fully detached and is unreachable. runc calls pivot_root(".", ".") from inside the new rootfs; runsc's gofer uses it to confine itself to the container root.

chroot changes only the calling process's root directory for path resolution. Escapes exist for privileged processes, so containers prefer pivot_root. The gVisor Sentry chroots into an empty directory so it cannot name any host path at all.

overlayfs merges read-only lower directories with a writable upper directory. It uses a workdir for atomic copy-up, whiteout device nodes for deletions and the trusted.overlay.opaque xattr for replaced directories. Pod: containerd's overlayfs snapshotter builds every container rootfs this way. Actor: Substrate's image cache composes cached layers plus an actor-private upper.

fsopen, fsconfig, fsmount, move_mount form the descriptor-based mount API added in Linux 5.2. fsopen("overlay") returns a filesystem context, fsconfig sets each option (lowerdir, upperdir, workdir) separately, avoiding the page-size limit of a single option string, fsmount creates a detached mount object, and move_mount attaches it. Actor: bundle_linux.go uses this sequence for actor root filesystems.

mount (command) and findmnt show and change mounts from a shell; /proc/self/mountinfo is the authoritative per-namespace mount table that both commands read.

Hard links, rename, renameat2(RENAME_EXCHANGE), unlink. A hard link is another name for the same inode, and the inode is freed when the last name and the last open descriptor are gone. rename atomically replaces one name. RENAME_EXCHANGE atomically swaps two names. Substrate uses hard links to share golden snapshot and asset files, and RENAME_EXCHANGE to publish a fetched asset (exchange_linux.go). containerd's content store uses rename to commit verified blobs.

cgroups

cgroup v2 filesystem. Resource control is a hierarchy of directories under /sys/fs/cgroup. mkdir creates a cgroup and rmdir removes an empty one, reparenting its charges. Writing a PID to cgroup.procs moves a process, and writing to cgroup.subtree_control enables controllers for children. Pod: the kubelet (directly or through systemd) creates QoS and Pod slices, and runc creates the container scope. Actor: the worker delegates the worker container's scope and creates worker, <uid>-_sandbox and transient <uid>-_ckpt leaves; runsc uses the sandbox leaf named in the OCI specification.

cpu.max, cpu.weight set a quota per period (for example 100000 100000 = one CPU) and a proportional share. memory.max is a hard limit that triggers reclaim and then the OOM killer. memory.high is a throttling threshold that applies heavy reclaim pressure but does not kill; Substrate swaps the sandbox's memory.max for memory.high so an actor at its limit slows down instead of dying. pids.max limits task count.

PSI (memory.pressure, cpu.pressure, io.pressure) reports the share of time tasks were stalled on a resource. The worker's memory watcher uses memory pressure, together with memory.events.local (counts of high, max and OOM events in this cgroup only), to decide when to intervene.

cgroup.kill kills every process in a cgroup atomically by writing 1. The worker's memory guard uses it to terminate an actor whose sandbox stays over its memory threshold.

systemd scopes and slices. With the systemd cgroup driver, the kubelet and runc ask systemd over D-Bus to create .slice and .scope units instead of creating directories directly; the names kubepods-burstable-pod<uid>.slice and cri-containerd-<id>.scope come from this.

Security and privilege

Capabilities and capset. Root's powers are split into about forty capabilities. A process has permitted, effective, inheritable, bounding and ambient sets. capset changes the first three, and prctl(PR_CAPBSET_DROP) removes entries from the bounding set permanently. runc applies the container's capability set this way. Substrate's worker Pods receive an explicit capability list from the WorkerPool controller instead of privileged mode.

prctl(PR_SET_NO_NEW_PRIVS) guarantees that execve can never grant more privileges, so set-UID binaries and file capabilities stop working. It is required for unprivileged seccomp filters. runc sets it for containers; the Sentry and gofer report NoNewPrivs: 1.

seccomp / prctl(PR_SET_SECCOMP) installs a BPF program that inspects every system call's number and arguments and returns allow, ERRNO, KILL, TRAP (deliver SIGSYS) or USER_NOTIF. Pod: runc installs the runtime's default profile when RuntimeDefault is selected. Actor: runsc installs filters on the Sentry and gofer limiting them to the host calls they need, and systrap uses SECCOMP_RET_TRAP in stub processes to divert application syscalls to the Sentry. The worker Pod itself runs with seccomp Unconfined.

AppArmor and SELinux are Linux Security Modules that confine programs by profile or label. runc selects the profile by writing to /proc/self/attr/apparmor/exec before execve. Substrate's worker Pods run AppArmor Unconfined; the inner sandbox's confinement comes from gVisor.

setuid, setgid, setgroups, setresuid change the process's user and group identity. runc calls them last, after operations that needed root, so the workload runs as the image or Pod user.

prctl(PR_SET_CHILD_SUBREAPER) makes a process adopt orphaned descendants instead of PID 1 of the namespace. containerd shims use it to collect exit statuses. Substrate's worker PID 1 (pid1.go) uses it to reap runsc helpers.

prctl(PR_SCHED_CORE) manages core scheduling cookies so tasks from different trust domains do not run simultaneously on sibling hyperthreads. The worker queries support and enables runsc core tags when available.

Processes and signals

execve replaces the calling process's program with a new one, keeping its PID, namespaces, cgroup and descriptors not marked close-on-exec. It is the last step of runc's init. Under gVisor, application programs are loaded by the Sentry's own ELF loader; the host execve runs only runtime binaries.

wait4 / waitid collect a child's exit status and release its zombie entry. The pause container, containerd shims and Substrate's PID 1 all reap with these calls.

kill, tgkill, signals. SIGTERM requests graceful shutdown and SIGKILL forces it. The kubelet's grace period is implemented by the shim sending one and then the other. runsc kill delivers signals to tasks inside the Sentry rather than to host processes.

pidfd_open, pidfd_send_signal, poll on a pidfd. A pidfd is a file descriptor that refers to one specific process. It becomes readable when that process exits and can be used to signal it without the risk of hitting a recycled PID. The worker opens a pidfd for each Sentry (pidfd.go).

pause() suspends the caller until a signal arrives. The pause container's main loop is a call to pause() in an infinite loop.

Networking

rtnetlink is the socket-based kernel interface (AF_NETLINK, NETLINK_ROUTE) for links, addresses, routes and neighbours. RTM_NEWLINK creates interfaces such as veth and bridge, or changes them: up/down, master, namespace through IFLA_NET_NS_FD. RTM_NEWADDR assigns addresses and RTM_NEWROUTE adds routes. The ip command is a client of rtnetlink. Pod: CNI plugins. Actor: the worker's sandbox.go.

ip link, ip addr, ip route are the commands for the same operations: ip link add a type veth peer name b, ip link set b netns X, ip addr add 10.0.0.2/24 dev b, ip route add default via 10.0.0.1. They are the manual equivalent of what a CNI plugin or the worker does programmatically.

veth pair is two virtual Ethernet devices joined back to back, so a frame sent into one comes out of the other. With the ends in different namespaces, it is the standard way to connect a namespace to the outside. Pods use one end as eth0. Each actor uses a pair between its runtime namespace (eth0) and its gateway namespace (atside).

Linux bridge is an in-kernel layer-2 switch. Bridge-style CNI plugins attach each Pod's host-side veth to a node bridge such as cni0. Actors do not use a bridge; their gateway namespace terminates traffic in atunnel.

iptables / nftables are the kernel's packet-filtering and NAT frameworks; nftables is the newer one, programmed with the nft command or netlink. Kubernetes uses them for Services (kube-proxy) and for CNI masquerading. Substrate's worker installs per-actor nftables tables that drop forwarding, reject link-local and non-TCP traffic, and redirect TCP to atunnel's port 15001.

conntrack and SO_ORIGINAL_DST. NAT state is kept in the connection-tracking table. A program that accepts a redirected connection can call getsockopt(SOL_IP, SO_ORIGINAL_DST) to learn the destination the client originally dialled. atunnel uses this to route actor egress (original_dst_linux.go).

sysctl and /proc/sys/net. Many network settings, such as ip_forward, arp_notify and rp_filter, are per network namespace and are set by writing files under /proc/sys/net while inside the namespace. CNI plugins and the worker both do this.

Packet sockets (AF_PACKET). These send and receive raw frames on an interface. gVisor's netstack, in sandbox networking mode, uses the namespace's interface this way, so the TCP/IP state lives in the Sentry rather than in the host kernel.

Unix domain sockets carry local RPC between processes on one host: the CRI socket, containerd shims' ttrpc sockets, atelet's worker sockets per Pod UID, WorkerSupport and the object-store plugin. They also carry file descriptors between processes (SCM_RIGHTS), which is how the gVisor gofer donates host files to the Sentry.

Memory and files

mmap / munmap map files or anonymous memory into an address space. The Sentry maps its memory file into stub address spaces; restore maps image data back into it.

memfd_create creates an anonymous, memory-backed file with no path. gVisor uses one as the memory file that backs all application memory, which is what makes memory checkpointing a matter of saving one file's populated ranges.

fallocate and madvise reserve or punch holes in file space, and advise the kernel about memory usage (for example MADV_DONTNEED to release pages). A user-space kernel uses calls of this kind to manage its memory file. The exact set belongs to the runsc release.

userfaultfd and UFFDIO_COPY. These let a user-space handler service page faults for a registered memory region: faults arrive as messages on a file descriptor, and the handler supplies the page contents with UFFDIO_COPY. Cloud Hypervisor's OnDemand restore uses this to load guest memory lazily. Substrate's microVM path selects it only conditionally; its gVisor path does not use it.

sync_file_range starts or waits for writeback of a file range without flushing metadata or disk caches. The worker uses it to make checkpoint pages clean, and therefore reclaimable, quickly (snapshotcache.go).

fsync / fdatasync flush a file's data (and, for fsync, its metadata) to stable storage. etcd and PostgreSQL rely on them for commit durability. They are the durability primitives; sync_file_range is not.

cachestat reports how many of a file's pages are cached, dirty, under writeback, evicted or recently evicted. It was added in Linux 6.5. The worker polls it to know when checkpoint files no longer occupy dirty memory.

posix_fadvise(POSIX_FADV_DONTNEED) asks the kernel to drop clean cached pages of a file range. The worker uses it after checkpoint writeback and after background restore to avoid keeping redundant image pages.

lseek(SEEK_DATA / SEEK_HOLE) finds the next populated region or hole in a sparse file. atelet's sparse helpers use it to transfer only populated extents of memory images.

copy_file_range copies bytes between two files inside the kernel, letting filesystems share extents (reflink) or avoid copying through user space. atelet uses it when materializing sparse captures.

Operator commands used in these chapters

kubectl is the Kubernetes API client; kubectl ate is Substrate's plugin speaking ateapi's gRPC API. crictl speaks CRI to containerd and shows Pod sandboxes, containers and images as the kubelet sees them. ctr speaks containerd's native API and shows content, snapshots and tasks. runc and runsc are the OCI runtimes. Running runsc --root <dir> list with the worker's per-actor state root lists the containers of one actor. nsenter, ip, nft, ss and findmnt inspect namespaces, networking, sockets and mounts. Under gVisor, ss and ip route see only the host side, because the actor's sockets live in the Sentry.
